profile: Bradley possesses a nice arm with clean mechanics. He made a few pretty deep passes over the past two years, mostly outside the numbers. His fundamentals allow him to maximize his arm talent, which is average for the NFL level. His athleticism allows him to scramble and pick up first downs. He also is not afraid to step up in the pocket. His game starts to fall off when he is asked to throw with touch on short or intermediate throws; his mechanics break down and he looks uncomfortable. He also tends to lock onto his primary read. Bradley's smaller hands also impact ball security and ball placement.
strengths: Won't be a dual threat, but can pick up yards with his legs when not accounted for Arm strength is average for the NFL. Throws with solid velocity thanks to a compact, clean motion. Tape contains a handful of very impressive deep throws from 45-55 yards over the past two years. Not afraid to step up in the pocket, even if he's taking a hit.
weaknesses: Has to put his whole body into throwing the fastball. Feels the need to always throw the fastball. Lacks touch when the situation calls for it. Smaller hands lead to some ball security issues. Struggles with the natural feel for touch passes. Mechanics break down when he tries to take speed off. Sometimes gets tunnel vision during his progressions.
bottom_line: Bradley is an intriguing prospect with a decent arm, an encouraging play style and good mechanics. How quickly he can learn to read NFL defenses and how much he can improve on touch throws is his key to locking down a preferred backup spot.

profile: Daniels' scouting report starts with his mobility. His success on RPOs and when scrambling means the defense has to account for his legs at all times. As for his passing, he is a very fundamentally sound thrower with light footwork, fluid hips and a repeatable follow-through. This, plus his overall arm talent, yields adequate velocity to all three levels. His touch in and out of structure has the potential for big plays. He is still speeding up his processing, which resulted in a high sack rate over the years, and he needs to protect himself more when tucking to run.
strengths: Legitimate rushing threat. He has adequate arm talent for all three levels of the field. Has decent velocity for middle-of-the-field throws, though distance is more impressive than velocity. Fundamentally sound throws from his feet to his follow-through. Excellent escapability to extend plays and beat blitzes — forces defenders to keep a spy.
weaknesses: Just one season of high-level production He needs to slide and avoid hits more often Velocity is just adequate Pocket presence is still a work in progress — very high sack rate. Processing speed did improve in 2023, but he is still a tick slow. Accuracy and ball placement can be inconsistent, but it stems from being a little late to see than a lack of talent.
bottom_line: Daniels' rushing ability and fundamentals give him a high floor as a player who can put a ton of stress on a defense. His arm talent is adequate to give him a decently high ceiling and makes him a worthy first round bet to make.

profile: Hartman's arm talent is well below average. His lack of arm strength requires his receivers to earn the kind of separation that just doesn't typically exist in the NFL. He has to put his entire body into throws beyond 45-50 yards, and when throwing off-platform, he does not have the upper body strength to put adequate velocity on passes. He can be accurate when throwing in rhythm and on schedule, but even then, he is limited, as he cannot consistently attack the intermediate middle of the field due to his lack of velocity.
strengths: Added mobility to be a decent RPO threat. Feet are light and bouncy. Can hang tough in the pocket and go through progressions when his protection allows it.
weaknesses: Does not have the height or the arm strength to attack over the middle of the field. He has to put his whole body into throws beyond 45 yards. Throws on his toes often due to lack of height. Off-platform throws have well below average velocity.
bottom_line: Hartman is an experienced quarterback with some decent mobility, but overall, he lacks the arm strength to become a starter or preferred backup in the NFL.

profile: Leary shows consistent technique in his throwing motion and footwork for some pretty passes. He is light on his feet and does a decent job of establishing a strong base to throw. Overall, his arm talent is adequate, as he does show the required velocity for hole shots versus Cover 2 in addition to tight-window passes over the middle of the field. Despite consistent mechanics, Leary's true ball placement is lacking. His accuracy also dips when he is moved off his spot and out of the pocket. When it comes to reading a defense, he struggles to see the whole picture against zone and puts the ball in harm's way too often.
strengths: Adequate arm strength for the NFL level. Has the velocity to hit outside throws. Clean throwing mechanics. Light on his feet and understands how to reset his base to throw. Willing to hang tough in the pocket under pressure.
weaknesses: Inconsistent ball placement, even within the offense's structure. Accuracy really dips when he is moved off his spot. Not afraid to let it loose down the sideline, but he just doesn't hit them enough. Struggles to see the whole picture of zone coverage — puts the ball in harm's way. Locks in on primary read too often.
bottom_line: Leary is a soothing, under-control passer with reliable mechanics, but his lack of playmaking ability and accuracy when things break down limits his ceiling.

profile: Maye's scouting reports start with his superb arm talent. He has a quick trigger to get the ball out of his hand fast. That comes with a lot of velocity to rip throws of any distance through tight coverage. His out-of-structure accuracy and touch are top-tier but can be inconsistent, which leads to Maye's biggest issue: ball placement. It doesn't seem to be a glaring footwork or motion issue, but he just simply misses throws at times. He has plus mobility and is experienced at attacking the middle of the field. He is also willing to go through progressions in a spread formation but is still improving on where to look and when.
strengths: Light on his feet — always bouncing and ready to pivot to progressions, throw or take off. Powerful flick of the wrist leads to good velocity. Has speed for escapability and scrambles. Capable of impressive out-of-structure accuracy. Experienced middle-of-the-field passer. Already well-versed in the pump fake to fool defenders.
weaknesses: There are times when he just misses, which can be due to a lack of fundamentals, but sometimes he just misses throws of varying distances. Fully capable and willing to read the full field, but he is still working on where to look and when.
bottom_line: Maye's arm talent alone puts him in the first-round and top-10 conversation. Though his ball placement and decision-making (including sacks taken) need improvement, he has all the talent tools you want to bet on as a franchise QB.

profile: McCarthy comes from a pro-style offense. As a first-time starter in 2022, he struggled to get off his primary read, fell for sim pressures and didn't have good instincts when pressured. In 2023, all of that improved, though that improvement needs to continue. His arm talent is good, both for velocity and natural accuracy. However, he does need to continue to get stronger to get his arm talent to an NFL level. His throwing motion is clean and efficient, from his footwork to his follow-through. You won't build a rushing attack around his mobility, but he is a good athlete who is a threat on RPOs and scramble plays.
strengths: Good, clean throwing motion. He has good arm talent but needs to continue to get stronger and put on weight to maximize it. Added mobility. Not afraid of tight-window throws, including over the middle. No reservations about throwing to the middle of the field. He can hang tough in the pocket.
weaknesses: Slender build — he must continue to get stronger He can get locked onto his primary reads. His decision-making took a step forward in 2023, but it needs to become more consistent, especially pre-snap.
bottom_line: McCarthy is not a finished product, but he is a growing quarterback with experience in a pro-style offense and good tools (physical and mental) to be a starting QB in the NFL.

profile: Milton is as physically gifted as they come at 6-foot-5 and 235 pounds with good mobility and a cannon of an arm. He operates almost exclusively from the shotgun in Vol’s wide formation vertical offense. His trump card is his arm talent. He is also useful in the power/RPO run game. However, he still has a ways to go as a passer before becoming a potential NFL starter. His feet are heavy and can stop moving when he's scanning the field. He also tends to get tunnel vision on primary reads and fails to move on in his progressions. His accuracy when throwing the fastball can be good, but his overall ball placement with touch is far too inconsistent.
strengths: Rocket launcher of an arm — he will have one of the strongest arms in the league when he gets drafted. Can contribute to the power/RPO run game immediately. Confident throwing outside the numbers, especially intermediate/deep.
weaknesses: Feet can sometimes stop moving as he scans the field. Accuracy can be serviceable, but true ball placement is low/late —his feet play a role in this. Accuracy falters when throwing with touch. Locks on to his primary reads often. Gets tunnel vision when scanning the field — loses timing of progressions and can sometimes not feel pressure around him.
bottom_line: Milton has NFL-level tools but lacks the processing, instincts and accuracy to be considered a potential starter in his current state.

profile: Some see Nix's age as a negative, but it has made him one of the more knowledgeable QB prospects with a better pre-snap understanding of defenses than most QBs. When the ball comes out of his hands, it has a consistent pace with good control. His pocket presence is good, but he could stand to climb the pocket more instead of fading away. He is an above-average athlete for the position and is always a threat to keep an RPO or scramble. As a passer, he is also accurate out of structure. He gets in trouble due to his footwork, as his feet are not as light as they could be. His knack for avoiding negative plays, including sacks, is top of the class.
strengths: Arm strength is adequate for the NFL level. Mobility is definitely a plus to his game. Good feel for the pocket/pressure and where to go with the ball afterward. Does well to avoid negative throws and not take sacks — smart player.
weaknesses: He has a bad habit of fading away when he doesn't need to. His feet aren't always married with his upper body. Sometimes they are too heavy, which is when his accuracy can dip I don't mind the quick-pass offense, but he does rely on the first read too often. He could stand to climb the pocket more.
bottom_line: Nix's experience manifests in the form of pre-snap reads, play under pressure and avoiding negatives. His footwork needs to be more disciplined, and he will take some time to really read progressions better in the NFL. However, he is a QB with starting-caliber tools in his arm and his legs, and he comes with added out-of-structure playmaking.

profile: Penix has been a productive quarterback in Washington's Air Raid system over the last two years. He shows off NFL-caliber distance and velocity on a variety of different throws, mostly outside the numbers. Penix can attack the intermediate middle of the field, but it is not as natural. He also tends to throw with power too much. He can be a tick late on timing his throws, opting to put more juice on passes rather than more air underneath. This lends itself to a lack of consistent ball placement. He also opts for the bigger throws and not as many "layups" even when available.
strengths: Has starting-caliber NFL arm strength in distance and velocity. No hesitation to give his players a deep shot. Strong sideline thrower — most of his production comes from throws outside the numbers.
weaknesses: Long arms require a longer/sidearm windup. Does not always throw with a strong base — sometimes, he’s pushing the ball with all upper body strength. Completion rate is fine, but true ball placement is inconsistent. Little volume or success over the intermediate middle of the field. Flamethrower arm strength leads to too much heat on his throws, at times — he could stand to use more timing and touch.
bottom_line: Penix Jr. has an NFL-level arm talent in addition to two years of good health and top-tier production in a spread-out shotgun offense. However, to become a consistent starter and top-15 quarterback in the league, he will need to clean up his footwork, throw with more anticipation and touch (which will improve ball placement), as well as be willing to attack the middle of the field.

profile: Plumlee is a great athlete for the position. He is agile, balanced and explosive enough to be a legit threat in an RPO offense. He can escape the pocket well, but his college passing grade when scrambling wasn't stellar. That stems from his lacking size at the position in height, weight and hand size. That combination will seriously limit his arm talent in the NFL. Even on clean passes, the ball wobbles to his target due to a lack of grip. Ole Miss' and UCF's offenses also did not ask him to go through progressions and read the field as much as other programs would, and thus, he recorded a high scramble rate and time to throw.
strengths: Very agile and elusive. Can pick up a lot of yards with his legs. Passing profile was much improved from 2022 to 2023. Threw with more confidence and accuracy.
weaknesses: Small in every major area for the position — height, weight and hand size. Struggles to grip and control the ball due to his hand size. Negatively affects accuracy. UCF’s offense limited how much he read the field. Lacks true NFL arm strength.
bottom_line: Plumlee is a good athlete who will likely make his biggest NFL contributions as a receiver or a quarterback in special packages.

profile: Plummer is a college football journeyman who played for three programs across six seasons. He stands tall in the pocket at 6-foot-4 and has good finesse for a big quarterback. His touch passes are some of the best in the class — over the middle, to the sideline and at the intermediate and deep levels of the field. He can really drop passes in a bucket. But that was out of necessity rather than him showing off true arm control, as he has below-average NFL arm strength. His accuracy numbers are good, but his true ball placement is lacking. Plummer also needs to more consistently step up in the pocket instead of retreating.
strengths: Tape features some excellent touch throws to the sideline and over the middle. His process looks great when he goes through progressions correctly. Has a full follow-through on touch passes.
weaknesses: While his accuracy scores are good, true ball placement is lacking. Misses high quite a bit. Does not step up in the pocket consistently when he needs to. Tends to retreat naturally. Arm power is well below the NFL average, even on on-platform throws.
bottom_line: Plummer has some of the best touch throws in the class, but when asked to fire up the arm strength to an NFL level, he leaves you wanting more. He is likely a practice squad or depth quarterback in the NFL.

profile: Pratt won't "wow" you with arm talent, but he does make up for that with clean fundamentals. His feet are light and his follow-through is consistent. After suffering a knee injury that kept him out three games in 2023, he did not return the same player. His velocity and power decreased when throwing, and his accuracy was off. His hands are small, which does cause some wobble in his throws. At times, he demonstrates how to manipulate coverages, but his decision-making can still be a tad slow. He also is quicker to take off and run than he needs to be. When attacking the middle of the field, he can hit vertical (seam) and horizontal (dig) routes.
strengths: Very clean fundamentals. Touch passes are a strength of his game —he's not afraid to put some air under his passes for his receivers. Not afraid to look to the middle of the field for seam or dig routes. Got better/more consistent manipulating coverage with his eyes in 2023.
weaknesses: Ball does wobble, at times, due to smaller hands. Arm strength is average. He has to really lean back to put distance on deeper passes. Chooses to take off and run instead of hitting shorter passes.
bottom_line: Pratt's clean fundamentals and impressive touch throws make him an intriguing quarterback, even with smaller measurables. His arm strength limits his ability to push the ball vertically, but he has a good enough feel for the game to garner a potential starter label.

profile: Rattler's time at Oklahoma was a roller coaster of high and low plays, but since transferring to South Carolina, he has become a more mature player. His preferred style comes in a shotgun system (over 85% of his snaps) with spread formations. He has adequate arm talent for the NFL level, though his velocity isn't the top tier. He has clean fundamentals, especially in his lower half. His protection was terrible in 2023, as he was pressured on almost 40% of his dropbacks. Despite that, his pocket presence is at an NFL level. Though he sees coverage well, he does struggle to see secondary defenders (LBs and safeties).
strengths: Really good footwork — feet are light and bouncy, a good base to start his throwing motion. Not much of a rushing threat, but he has a good enough feel for the pocket/coverage to take yards with his legs when presented. Pocket presence is much improved from his Oklahoma days. Conscious to reset once moved off his spot. Not afraid to attack over the intermediate middle of the field.
weaknesses: Accuracy is good, but ball placement isn't at an elite/special level. Almost exclusively a shotgun quarterback. Arm talent is adequate, not top-tier. Struggles to see additional coverage players (LBs and safeties) beyond the primary player guarding his receiver. Post-snap decision-making is still improving (where to scramble, where to look, timing of getting to his next read, etc.).
bottom_line: Rattler has a mature game with fundamentals and pocket presence, in addition to good accuracy in and out of structure. His arm is adequate, but he needs to continue to improve at seeing additional coverage defenders post-snap. He projects as a Day 2 QB with starting potential.

profile: Reed wasn't always destined for the NFL. As a zero-star recruit, he went from Southern Illinois to West Florida before landing at WKU for his final two years. He is a confident player who will set and make tight-window throws on different platforms. He oozes that "gamer" vibe. His lack of arm talent was the main reason he was under-recruited. He has clean throwing mechanics, helping maximize velocity and distance. But even then, he has to put his whole body into throws to generate enough velocity. He throws the fastball too much, as touch passes are not his game. His ball placement is also erratic (likely stemming from full-body throws).
strengths: "Gamer" type of quarterback. He is willing to throw off-platform and outside the offense's structure. Clean follow-through on his throwing motion leads to some pretty passes, which helps make up for his lack of true arm strength. Confident passer in WKU's offense. Willing to attempt some tight- window intermediate passes. Willing to attack the middle of the field.
weaknesses: Holds the ball lower when scanning the field. Has a long wind-up. Has below-average arm talent. Puts a lot of his body behind passes to increase their velocity. Every pass is a fastball — struggles when he has to throw with touch. Ball placement is an issue — recorded just a 52.4% adjusted completion percentage beyond five yards.
bottom_line: Reed has a moxie that some teams could like enough to make him an early Day 3 pick, but his lack of passing traits and natural touch make him a backup-only player.

profile: Slovis is an experienced quarterback who burst onto the scene with an electric true freshman season at USC. Unfortunately, he didn't maintain that level of production and efficiency, which sent him on a college football journey to Pittsburgh and then BYU. Slovis' arm talent is well below average for the NFL level. He has good athletic mobility but fails to make the right reads/plays outside of structure. He also has a bad tendency to drift deeper in the pocket instead of stepping up. Ultimately, his lack of consistent accuracy holds him back from being a rosterable quarterback.
strengths: Decent mobility to get out of the pocket when pressured. Can make nice touch/timing throws to the sideline. Clean and quick upper-body mechanics.
weaknesses: Struggles to keep composure under pressure. Gets tunnel vision and fails to see additional defenders. Arm talent is below average for the NFL. Natural reaction is to retreat in the pocket instead of stepping up. Follow-through footwork can be erratic, as his leg tends to kick out wide.
bottom_line: Slovis has ample experience but not enough production, intangibles or passing traits to be a potential starter or preferred backup at the NFL level.

profile: Tagovailoa transferred to Maryland, where he became a school and conference record holder. His pro traits don't match his college production, though. Taulia is very small compared to other NFL quarterbacks, which leads to a lack of overall arm talent. His throwing mechanics are unorthodox — from his frenetic footwork to his side-armed throwing motion. Though it works at times, its inconsistencies yield far too much variance with ball placement. He does bring mobility for scrambles and extending plays outside the pocket.
strengths: Fiesty player who won't give up on a play until he is brought down. Not afraid to take a deep shot down the sideline. Brings added mobility to extend plays and pick up yards when scrambling.
weaknesses: Bryce Young-type measurables. Has a side-arm follow-through, which works, at times, but doesn't feel consistent. Long, looping throwing motion (akin to Tim Tebow). Accuracy scores are high, but ball placement is far more inconsistent.
bottom_line: Tagovailoa is a decent athlete and a fun playmaker out of structure, but his lack of size and true arm talent, coupled with passing inconsistencies, makes him a long shot at the NFL level.

profile: Travis is a good athlete who can operate an RPO and play- action offense well. His mobility is also a plus for escaping the pocket via scrambles. He is one of the smaller quarterbacks in the class, which brings natural drawbacks. His hand size is concerning when controlling the ball. He also tends to have to put his whole body into throws that require more juice. His follow-through is erratic, as he will kick his leg out like a pitcher to generate more velocity. He has good intangibles. He is accurate and poised when throwing out of structure, and he doesn't mind throwing over the middle, even if he has to be on his toes.
strengths: He has impressive mobility. Footwork is light, as he's constantly bouncing and ready to throw or take off. Keeps his eyes downfield when scrambling. Not afraid to look over the middle despite the lack of size. Accurate thrower from within 50 yards (when his follow-through fundamentals don't betray him).
weaknesses: Leg kicks out like a pitcher when he's trying to put extra juice on throws. Flicks the wrist sometimes, especially when off-platform, instead of following through. He has to put his whole body into passes that will be regular throws in the NFL.
bottom_line: Travis is a good athlete, a tough competitor, and a QB who has great intangibles for out-of-structure plays. His follow-through fundamentals are a mess, likely due to him needing more power on most throws, which leads to inconsistencies. He is a developmental quarterback who will be a fan favorite no matter where he goes (likely on Day 3).

profile: Williams thrived over the last three seasons in Lincoln Riley's modernized Air Raid offense. His arm talent is well above average, and his footwork provides him with a good base in addition to additional body control and balance to make off- platform throws. His accuracy is natural and impressive both in and out of structure. Williams can hold onto the ball too long, but that's due to his freedom in a vertical offense rather than an inability to process. His 2023 struggles were due to inconsistency. His fearless confidence does lead to some incorrect decisions, but you live with that due to the magic he makes in similar situations.
strengths: Top-tier arm talent for the NFL level. Incredible off-script passer and playmaker. Footwork is good in its fundamental base Top-tier balance, body control and core strength. Excellent out-of-structure touch. Very competitive player. Better processor/progressions passer than given credit for. Turns into a backyard playmaker when he tucks to run..
weaknesses: Has a tendency to look for the "biggest" throw instead of the "best" throw. His fearlessness is a big positive for huge plays, but it also leads to him holding onto the ball too long. Fewer big-time throws in structure, but that isn't due to a lack of ability.
bottom_line: Williams is an incredibly talented player with natural gifts even other previous QB1s do not have. His issues are more from a lack of consistency than ability in any area. This is a QB with franchise-changing talent that is worthy of a No. 1 overall selection.

profile: Ali has a nice skill set for a zone-blocking scheme. He reads his aiming points and cut-back lanes well and has good one- cut ability to hit open space. He has solid footwork to stay balanced after ankle tackles but lacks the density to bounce off contact. Over the past two seasons, his production beyond his blockers was subpar in the form of yards after contact and missed tackles forced. Though he has good burst, his top speed is limited.
strengths: Good skill set for a zone-blocking scheme. Has good vision/feel for cut-back lanes behind zone blocking. Nice change-of-direction precision and burst. Fast feet to maintain balance after ankle tackles.
weaknesses: Low individual production beyond his offensive line. Low yards after contact and missed tackles forced averages. Lacks density to truly bounce off tacklers. Pass blocking is still a work in progress.
bottom_line: Ali has good vision and one-cut ability to succeed as a depth player in a zone-blocking scheme.

profile: Allen will be one of the youngest players in the 2024 draft, 20 years old on draft weekend. His size pops out immediately at 6-foot-2 and 245 pounds. If you try to tackle him high, he'll bounce right off you with good tackle-breaking ability. He has nimble feet and impressive burst for his size. His long speed is also fine. His vision and decision-making are inconsistent, as he cuts in when he should bounce out and vice versa. For third-down abilities, his hands are good enough to be a receiving option, but his route diversity out of the backfield is limited. He has the size to be a good pass protector but needs more consistency there as well.
strengths: He is a very good linear athlete for his size. Explosiveness and top speed are NFL caliber, even without weight adjustments. Can't bring him down if you hit him high. Pass protection potential is a big plus. Not used as a receiver much but had some nice grabs (a few one -handed ones).
weaknesses: Not a one-cut back in space. Vision and feel for open space can be inconsistent. Usage and route diversity are very limited.
bottom_line: Allen is a super-sized running back prospect and will likely be a mid-round pick due to that and his age alone. However, his decision-making and feel for space leave much to be desired when separating his success from his offensive line.

profile: Benson's track speed shows up immediately on tape, as his acceleration and top speed are both excellent. His explosiveness allows him to covert speed-to-power to break tackles. He is a bit stiff when it comes to changing direction and agility. His athletic advantage is a good thing, but it does affect his mentality, vision and patience for rush lanes. He is overeager to get to the sideline and outrun defenders rather than find a cutback lane. This works at the college level but won't be as effective in the NFL. As a pass catcher, he does let passes come into his body but is an option as a third- down back due to his pass-protection abilities.
strengths: Powerful build — good size/strength in his legs, Explosive athlete with difference-making burst and top speed, Can convert speed-to-power quickly for yards after contact. Fundamentally sounds pass blocker with a good base and the strength to hold up.
weaknesses: A little stiff in his lateral movements. Base is narrow, which makes it easier for him to get tripped up. High missed tackles forced is more about speed-to-power and erasing pursuit angles than it is one-cut elusiveness. Is an athlete first, so he tends to miss open cutback lanes in favor of getting to the sideline as soon as possible. Let passes get into the body.
bottom_line: Benson brings NFL build and athleticism to the table in all categories of explosiveness, but he is too focused on his athletic abilities and needs more patience in order to maximize his athletic gifts and be more than a committee running back.

profile: Brooks, a decorated Texas high school football player, had to wait his turn behind the likes of Bijan Robinson and Roschon Johnson before taking over as the Longhorns’ lead back in 2023. The wait appeared to be worth it, as he looked like a future NFL star as just a redshirt sophomore. While his footwork isn’t quite Robinson’s level, he can cut/change direction/avoid tacklers very quickly and has an explosive first step. He isn’t a nuanced route runner, but he has good hands and showcased his ability to force missed tackles as a receiver. The only glaring negative on his scouting report is a torn ACL in 2023 that ended his lone season as a starter.
strengths: Impressive wiggle for a back of his size. Nice footwork and change-of-direction for a back over 200 lbs. Good vision/feel for zone-blocking schemes. Contact balance is great at high and low speeds. Natural instincts for forcing missed tackles. Long speed isn't elite, but the burst is at his size. Natural hands in the receiving game. - Has the footwork and strength/balance to be a reliable blocker.
weaknesses: North-to-south tendency is good, but that has given him tunnel vision, at times. Hands are good as a receiver, but he doesn't have much nuance in routes before the ball.
bottom_line: Brooks is an ideal blend of size, speed, strength and agility. Though limited in snap totals, he has good vision in both gap and zone run schemes. If he can get back to form following his torn ACL, he has all the goods to be a starting running back in the NFL.

profile: Corum was one of the most productive backs in the country in 2022, and he was on his way to being a top-75 selection had he not torn his meniscus late in the season. He comes in a smaller size at 5-foot-8 but weighs around 210 pounds. The smaller frame means he has shorter strides, which does affect his overall long speed and sideline ability. However, they also help yield his calling card as a back: his precise footwork and elite short-area explosiveness. As a pass catcher, he has very natural hands. In pass protection, he is willing, but his lack of size causes him to be overwhelmed, at times.
strengths: Great center of gravity when taking on contact. Shorter frame allows him to be precise and explosive when putting his foot in the ground to burst or change direction. Very natural hands as a receiver. Smaller frame allows him to "get skinny" between the tackles Controlled, precise footwork behind the LOS and in space. Patience is a huge plus in his game. Willing as a blocker. Uses size for a leverage advantage.
weaknesses: Leg stride length affects his overall long speed. Just doesn't have that get-away top speed. Can be overwhelmed in pass protection.
bottom_line: Corum was not as efficient in the individual metrics of running back play after his meniscus tear, but the traits of an effective back were present in 2023, specifically toward the end of the season. He lacks elite overall athleticism but is precise, sees the field well, has good contact balance and brings good third- down abilities, which should yield a contributing role in the NFL.

profile: Davis was a tough matchup for FCS opponents, as he is big and elusive. His size allows him to bounce off tackles and lower his shoulders with power, and his feet are impressively light for his size. He is a patient runner, especially behind zone blocking, and has a good feel for cut-back lanes and space. His preferred running style is that of a "make you miss" player, which is both a pro and con. The pro is obviously the missed tackles, and the con is that he doesn't run with a north-to-south violence. He has good hands as a receiver, but his pass protection is a work in progress.
strengths: Patient player with a good understanding of zone blocking schemes. Light on his feet for a player well above the 50th percentile in height and weight. Good wiggle to make players miss in space. Can make an impact in the receiving game.
weaknesses: Doesn’t run as violently as he could. Not that he won't be physical, but he oesn't go all out north to south. Lacks the sideline athleticism needed for bouncing plays outside as much as he does.
bottom_line: Davis brings a finesse game in a power frame. If he can run with more violence from north to south, he can be a reliable option in a two-back offense.

profile: Davis is short, which affects his overall speed, but he has a great center of gravity in addition to nimble and balanced footwork. He also has a quick first step to accelerate and fantastic vision, especially when running behind a zone- blocking scheme. As a third-down back, he has good hands and brings that one-cut agility to routes out of the backfield. When it comes to pass protection, he is a willing blocker who has good fundamentals but is often overpowered.
strengths: Quick player with fast footwork. Good one-cut ability. Good lateral ability extends into routes out of the backfield as well. Playmaker mentality in space — wants to make defenders miss. Really nice vision for both gap and zone, but he is most productive when running zone concepts. Good hands catcher. Really good feel for space, blocking, where his help is, etc.
weaknesses: Long speed will be average at best — likely below average. Can get overwhelmed in pass protection.
bottom_line: Davis might not have the build and long speed of a back drafted in the top 50, but his vision, feel for space/blocking and one-cut ability make him an efficient ball carrier with good hands in the passing game. This should make him a mid-round selection and potential starter.

profile: At nearly 230 pounds, Estime is tough between the tackles. Once he gets up to speed, he's a load to bring down, especially since his big legs continue to churn after contact for an impressive yards-after-contact rate. The finesse parts of his game are limited. His burst and long speed will be merely average compared to other NFL backs, and though he is nimble behind the line of scrimmage, changing direction once up to speed takes multiple steps. As for third down, he was not used much as a receiver, but his pass-protection potential is good due to his size and strength. A big plus is he will be just 20 years old on draft weekend.
strengths: Great build for a back — powerful player who can take hits and deal them out. His legs are constantly churning, even after contact. Takes ball security very seriously. Pretty light on his feet for a player who is pushing 230 pounds. Has the ability to dance and cut behind the line of scrimmage. Has the size and strength to be a third-down back in pass pro.
weaknesses: Burst is middling, especially when compared to NFL backs. Won't be a home run back in the NFL due to average long speed. Stiff change of direction when he gets up to speed, as it takes multiple steps. Lacks the lateral ability to really succeed on zone concepts. Blocking could use more polished technique.
bottom_line: Estime's power profile should yield some sort of committee work at the NFL level, as he is built for it. However, his lack of finesse and speed likely limits him to a short-yardage specialist.

profile: Gore's best trait is his vision, as he displays notable patience behind the line of scrimmage while anticipating open space/blocking concepts well. He has quick, precise footwork that allows him to find small holes and rush lanes, in addition to making defenders miss at the line of scrimmage. Small in stature, he is a limited athlete in terms of burst and long speed. He is also unreliable in pass protection against NFL-caliber blitzers.
strengths: Very good patience and vision. Experience is evident on his tape. Quick, explosive footwork. Good one-cut ability for forcing missed tackles.
weaknesses: Shorter strides limit top speed. When he reaches open space, he doesn't have the top gear to get away. One-cut ability is nice, but his burst and acceleration are limited. Broke away from arm tackles at the C-USA level, but he likely doesn't have the size to do so in the NFL. Pass protection is unreliable against good blitzers.
bottom_line: Gore's vision and feel for the game are good enough to have him fighting for a roster spot at the next level, but his limited athleticism could force him into a depth rotational role.

profile: Though Guerendo is built like a Wisconsin back, he didn't get much of a chance to showcase that. He was primarily used as a third-down back, which helped him hone his pass-blocking and pass-catching abilities. Though he is big and fast, he doesn't run with the violence you'd expect. He can bounce off tackles, but he doesn't always run with an imposing style. He is also hesitant behind the line of scrimmage. He can erase angles when he gets to the sideline but tries to bounce it there too often.
strengths: Has the size and strength to be a reliable pass protector. Ample experience as a receiver out of the backfield. Brings a wide receiver background from high school. Very explosive straight-line athlete. Likes to get outside and erase angles up the sideline. Good strength and size to bounce off tackles.
weaknesses: Indecisive at Wisconsin, but he did show more north-to-south urgency at Louisville. Does not run with the level of violence you'd want, given his size. A bit stiff when moving laterally. Too reliant on beating defenders to the sideline — needs to see cut-back lanes better.
bottom_line: Guerendo has an NFL-level floor as a third-down back. He must continue to improve his vision and decisiveness to become an early-down contributor.

profile: Bucky Irving's compact build gives way to his most alluring trait: balance. His ability to run through arm tackles and bounce off bigger hits can give him a long career in the NFL. He doesn't have great long speed and won't be outrunning anyone at the sideline, but his footwork is quick, controlled and balanced while his burst is appropriate for his game. He also has very reliable hands out of the backfield, though his pass protection abilities are unreliable.
strengths: Doesn't have the best long speed but does have great burst to hit holes quickly. Fast, controlled, balanced footwork to make defenders miss in phone booth. Natural, reliable hands as a receiver. Nice center of gravity to bounce off tackles, consistently falls forward. Despite his size, he looks for yards between the tackles.
weaknesses: Very north-to-south runner, which can be good, but there are times when the outside is open but doesn't take it. Not a reliable pass blocker. Does not have getaway speed.
bottom_line: Irving might not have the look of a running back that teams will automatically covet on draft weekend, but his tape shows an incredibly efficient player in both the run and pass games.

profile: Johnson has good footwork speed for finding his blocks behind the offensive line and has notable acceleration once he does. Unfortunately, he just did not do much to create beyond his blocking scheme to stand out in this running back class — both his yards after contact and missed tackles forced rates fell below the 40th percentile over the last two years. On the plus side, he does have good third-down ability as a receiver and pass protector.
strengths: Fierce stiff arm. Has a decent foot speed to make people miss and cut in the backfield.
weaknesses: Long speed appears slightly above average. Doesn't really set defenders up to make them miss — doesn’t get much more than what's blocked for him. Takes a few steps for him to his cutbacks.
bottom_line: Johnson is a decent all-around athlete but lacks a difference- making trait for him to stand out at the NFL level. His most likely projection is as a third-down back.

profile: Laube’s lacrosse background shows in his natural movement skills. His short-area burst, footwork and balance are impressive and effective. Laube lacks true NFL size and power. His leg drive stalls out quickly against linebackers and yields a lower yards-after-contact average. It also shows up in a lack of NFL-level top gear for long speed. Between the tackles, he does show good vision and has a great ability to "get skinny" between blocks to find rush lanes.
strengths: Natural, reliable hands in the receiving game. Natural athleticism is evident in how he moves — balanced, precise and good short-area burst. Slippery between the tackles.
weaknesses: Doesn't have an NFL-level top gear. Lacks the desired leg drive for yards after contact at the NFL level.
bottom_line: Laube's receiving and special teams ability should yield a long NFL career, but his lack of true NFL size and power might limit his ceiling.

profile: Lloyd's calling card is his athletic ability. His burst, agility and long speed are all well above average for the NFL level. He's the kind of back who he can take it to the house if he gets to the sideline. His vision for finding those running lanes is still inconsistent, as he often fails to see cutback lanes in zone- blocking schemes. However, when running gap schemes, he does seem more patient. As a third-down back, he wasn't used much as a receiver, but he does have good hands and an electric after-the-catch ability. He is also one who takes pride in his blocking game to help other teammates.
strengths: NFL-level long speed and acceleration. Impressive all-around athleticism in terms of explosiveness and elusiveness. Maintains the ability to make players miss in space after the catch, as well. Adequate size and strength for pass protection. Has a good pass-protecting baseline.
weaknesses: Wants to bounce runs out the sideline too much — developed this more at USC. Does not see cutback lanes as fast/as often as he needs to for zone-blocking schemes.
bottom_line: Lloyd is a starting NFL-caliber athlete for the running back position. If he can improve his vision to see space before it opens up, he can be an impact starter.

profile: McClellan's best trait is his contact balance. He constantly works through contact, using his core strength, balance and leg drive. His speed is average for the NFL level, but it shouldn't be a detractor. He is a bit stiff in his lateral movement and can take a few steps to really cut behind zone blocks. As a receiver, he lets the ball come into his body too often. He is a willing pass blocker with some nice reps, but he has some bad tendencies — such as slow feet and dipping his head — that limit his reliability on third downs.
strengths: Weight is well distributed for good balance through contact. Strong leg drive for yards after contact. Repeatedly ran through arm tackles at the college level.
weaknesses: Sees space/future space just a tick slow. Cuts behind zone blocking can take a few steps. Average long speed for the NFL. Willing pass blocker, but feet can be slow to mirror, head will dip and he'll lose rushers. Lets passes come into the body too often. Not a natural receiver.
bottom_line: McClellan is a solid athlete with above-average contact balance to be a potential committee back in the NFL.

profile: Milton couldn't consistently showcase his talents over the past four years due to injuries. He is a big back with a strong north-to-south running style who works well behind man/gap blocking schemes. He doesn't possess the true flexibility and agility to be a consistent playmaker behind zone. He also lacks a playmaking mentality once he gets to open space. A lot of his best production stems from his offensive line. His first-step explosiveness is powerful, but his long speed is below average for the NFL. His experience as a receiver is basically non-existent; however, he is a willing and strong pass blocker with potential.
strengths: Coordinated, strong pass blocker. Good eyes for incoming rushers. Powerful back with good, but not elite, contact balance and leg drive. A lot of experience behind man/gap blocking schemes.
weaknesses: Doesn't show a playmaker's mentality when in open space. Seems to have only one speed: downhill ASAP. Powerful and explosive first step, but top gear is below average for NFL standards. Almost no experience as a receiver (eight targets in two years). Long list of injuries that have kept him off the field.
bottom_line: What you see is what you get with Milton, who is a strong north- to-south runner with plus pass-blocking ability. However, his injury history and lack of a true playmaker's mentality in space will likely limit him to depth back and special teams roles.

profile: Schrader's story of perseverance is mirrored in his running style, as he is a fiery competitor who has a motor that doesn't quit. His effort will earn him a shot on any roster — first as a willing pass protector on third downs. His vision and one-cut ability are effective enough to project success in zone- blocking schemes, though his lack of overall size and athleticism may lead to lower returns. His shorter strides do limit his top speed.
strengths: Determined and competitive running style. Coaches will love his motor and effort. Willing and fundamentally sound pass protector. Some of his best games were against top competition (Georgia, Tennessee, Ohio State). One-cut ability is very effective.
weaknesses: Smaller size impacts his pass-protection ability. Shorter stride length limits long speed. Change of direction when getting up to speed can be tight.
bottom_line: Schrader may lack the overall athleticism/size to be a consistent difference-maker beyond his offensive line, but he has everything else you'd want to try to make up for it: vision, elusiveness, determination and a physical run style.

profile: Shipley is a quick, versatile scatback who has impressive acceleration across his first few steps. He has limited top speed, but he can get to that top speed very quickly. He also has great body control and balance, which makes for a dangerous one-cut player who can get tripped up and regain his composure for more yards. He is also an excellent receiver who has soft hands and a lot of volume. The biggest issue with Shipley is his strength and overall body density. This also affects his pass-blocking effectiveness, as he is willing as a blocker but is easily overpowered.
strengths: 40 targets in each of the past two seasons speaks to how natural he is as a receiver. Footwork is quick and precise, which makes for smooth yet explosive cuts. Very nice balance for contact. Long speed is adequate, as his short burst is even better.
weaknesses: Willing pass blocker but doesn't have the necessary weight to be reliable. Has good balance and body control but lacks the strength to bounce off tackles.
bottom_line: Shipley can bring a lot of versatility to a team as a runner, receiver and special teammer. He is elusive and quick with a skill set fit for a zone blocking scheme, but right now, his lack of strength and power hold him back from being a true offensive weapon.

profile: Shirden went from a 0-star recruit to an impact player at Monmouth. He led the FCS in rushing in two consecutive season in 2022 and 2023 with over 3,200 yards and 23 touchdowns. Shirden is a high-speed playmaker who can process things quickly and stay one step ahead of defenders to make them miss in open space. He has good long speed and burst, and can even give you some decent leg drive despite being only 187 pounds. He is unreliable in third down back situations as both a reciever and pass protector. He can read zone blokcing schemes well, but man/gap concepts are not as natural to him.
strengths: Long speed is good for the NFL level (makes his competition at Monmouth look silly) Speed/burst allows him to shrug off arm tackles Good one cut ability for zone blocking schemes Still gives you some leg drive, even at just 187 pounds Quick processor who can make agile moves at high speeds
weaknesses: Will not be a third down back at the NFL level; unreliable in pass pro, inexperienced as a pass catcher Does not read man/gap schemes as well as he does zone
bottom_line: Shirden is a high speed processor with quick feet and good burst to be a potential speed back in a rotation behind zone blocking schemes.

profile: Steele was a standout rusher at Ball State before transferring to UCLA for the 2023 season. Though his rushing grade was higher in zone blocking schemes, his hard-nosed style better fits man/gap schemes. He is a compact, powerful player. He plays behind his pads, will lower the shoulder against anyone and will stiff-arm lighter defenders into the ground. His legs are always churning for extra yards. He is a bit stiff on one- cuts and when looking to make players miss in open space. His long speed will be well below average for the NFL level due to a shorter stride length. He has the strength and body type to be a reliable pass protector.
strengths: Compact, powerful frame. Will fight hard for every yard. Legs don't stop churning. Fierce stiff arm.
weaknesses: High missed tackles forced average comes more from breaking tackles than making players miss in space. Has the power to be reliable in pass protection, but his technique is inconsistent. Long speed will be well below average for the NFL. Shorter strides cap how much ground he covers.
bottom_line: Steele won't be a home-run hitter in the NFL, but he can be a short-yardage, third-down back with his powerful running style.

profile: Tracy spent most of his college football career at wide receiver but never made the impact he had envisioned. He has an upright running style but remains balanced on his feet for yards after contact. He has a make-you-miss running style due to good elusiveness and one-cut ability. His lack of experience at running back yields inconsistencies in how he reads blocks. On third downs, his hands and route running are impressive. Although he brings good length and a willingness to pass block, his strength and confidence are still hit or miss.
strengths: Natural athlete in whatever he's asked to do. Upright, tall running style but remains balanced through contact. Explosive and fast enough to get to and up the sideline. Experienced and talented receiver out of the backfield who can run any route. Natural make-you-miss type of running style — nicknamed himself "Sweet Feet" for that reason.
weaknesses: Good length but currently lacks strength/confidence in pass protection. Hands are inconsistent in pass protection. Inconsistent vision, which is understandable, given he’s played RB for one season.
bottom_line: Tracy is a natural playmaker with adequate athleticism (explosiveness and agility) for a zone-blocking scheme, but he must continue to improve how he sees blocks/space if he is to be a consistent rotational player.

profile: Vaki played both sides of the ball (running back, slot receiver, and safety) in high school due to his impressive athleticism. He was recruited in the 2019 class, so he is one of the older prospects, but he only has two years of college football experience due to a two-year church mission before playing football for Utah. Vaki does not have much experience as a running back at the college level, but what we saw from him in 2023 could absolutely contribute in the NFL. He has home run speed with fantastic play strength and contact balance. His route tree as a receiver is very simple, but what he does, he does very well.
strengths: As a receiver out of the backfield, his straight-line speed smokes most college linebackers on wheel routes. Precise route runner on Texas routes out of the backfield. An incredibly determined runner when it comes to yards after contact. Turns into a true playmaker when he gets the ball — his feet are fast and deceptive, as he always looking to make defenders miss. Has legitimate home run speed.
weaknesses: Does not have the nuances of the position simply from a lack of carries — will hold the ball in the wrong hand.
bottom_line: If he fully committed to playing running back in the NFL, he has the physical gifts, athletic ability and playmaker's vision to be a contributing player out of the backfield.

profile: Vidal rushed for more than 2,700 yards and 24 touchdowns over the past two seasons and recorded back-to-back elite rushing grades. He is an explosive, powerful running back with a rocked-up, compact frame. His scouting report starts with effort. His fight and mentality after contact are impressive, despite his not being the strongest back. He has above-average straight-line speed for the NFL but can be a bit stiff and take an extra gather step when pivoting. He still needs to speed up his vision. Too often he is slow to see developing space/blocking. On third downs, he is a good receiver but does not anticipate in pass protection well enough.
strengths: Explosive runner who wastes no time getting upfield. Long speed is above average for the NFL, but not elite. Not the strongest after-contact player, but his fight makes up for it.
weaknesses: A tick late to see space/blocking and to cut and make a decision. Agility is decent, but change of direction takes him an extra gather step to pivot and go. Unreliable in pass protection/ Doesn't anticipate/brace well enough.
bottom_line: Vidal is a rocked-up, explosive athlete, but his vision for space needs to speed up for him to earn a rotational role in the NFL.

profile: Watson started his college career as a wide receiver at Old Dominion and switched to running back in his third year before transferring to Memphis in 2023. He is at his best when he gets out to the sideline in wide-zone blocking schemes. This allows him to use his difference-making top speed and one-cut ability. His body control is impressive. He can stop on a dime with precision and explosiveness. His patience behind man/gap schemes needs work, but it is improving. He is an excellent receiver out of the backfield. He can fully extend for catches and is confident in his routes. Watson is a willing pass protector but could be more confident.
strengths: Adequate NFL explosiveness, both linearly and laterally. Ample receiving experience and nuance. Impressive body control to stop on a dime and change directions quickly and precisely. Nice balance to get yards after contact and stay on his feet.
weaknesses: Willing blocker, but not as confident as he needs to be when taking on rushers. Doesn't have as good of a feel for space between the tackles.
bottom_line: Watson is an alluring athlete out of the backfield, both as a rusher and a receiver. He should earn the versatile "offensive weapon" label with the potential to be an NFL contributor.

profile: Williams was the power player in Ohio State's running back rotation. Though he is smaller in height, he's nearly 230 pounds and carrys that weight well. His contact balance allows him to stay on his feet and churn out yards after contact. He is limited athletically by NFL standards. His burst, long speed and elusiveness will all be limiting factors in the league. Williams is confident in his north-to-south running style. He was seldom used in the receiving game and was unreliable in pass protection. Unfortunately, Williams underwent season-ending knee surgery in 2023, which further clouds his projection.
strengths: Good contact balance to stay on his feet. Strong center of gravity. Excels as a north-to-south back. Can get skinny between blockers for a power back. Controlled style with light footwork.
weaknesses: Does not provide much as a pass catcher. Season-ending knee surgery in 2023. Can be impatient getting to the line of scrimmage. Long speed and burst will be limiting factors in the NFL. Doesn't have the natural agility to make defenders miss in space consistently. Unreliable on third down as a blocker and receiver.
bottom_line: Williams is a no-nonsense north-to-south back whose production typically originated behind zone blocking concepts where he could get a head of steam and move past the line. His athletic limitations, looming knee rehab and lack of consistency in pass protection and as a receiver make him a fringe roster prospect.

profile: Wright brings plenty of speed and explosiveness to the running back position. At Tennessee, he became the team's leading rusher as a sophomore in 2022, and he wasn't even the Vols' lead back. His calling card is his explosiveness. His first step, whether that be linear or lateral, is eye-popping. He follows that up with an NFL-level top gear to eat up a ton of open space. As a receiver, he has good hands while his explosiveness makes for a sharp route runner. He was one of the best backs in the country in pass protection this past season due to his size and strength.
strengths: Top-tier athlete for the position. Explosive first step is very impressive, as he makes devastating cuts and can turn speed into power when taking on contact. Has legitimate long speed for the NFL. Is a reliable pass protector due to his play strength. Despite having sideline speed, he does show a decent amount of patience to set up blocks and stay between the tackles and within the blocking scheme.
weaknesses: Though he does have decent patience, he doesn't always see the open rush lanes when it's not the primary hole on the play. Catching ability is there, but he's not exactly natural. More hesitant of a runner after the catch than he is when he is handed the ball in the backfield.
bottom_line: Wright is an NFL-caliber athlete for the running back position. His youth is both a positive (lack of mileage) and a negative (lack of consistent RB vision), but he has succeeded in both gap and zone-blocking concepts and has top-tier pass protection ability for three-down potential in the NFL.

profile: Baker spent two years at Alabama but failed to crack the team's starting wide receiver group consistently, and he ultimately landed at UCF. His scouting report starts with his competitive nature. He is an outside receiver who doesn't back down from press coverage or tight-space catches along the sideline. His footwork and feel for small spaces are impressive. He also has very strong hands, helping him make spectacular catches through contact. He is explosive in short areas but lacks NFL-caliber long speed to consistently separate. Baker is also still mastering the art of finding soft spots versus zone.
strengths: Competitive player at the catch point and when fighting off press. Good hip fluidity to sharply change direction. Initial burst and acceleration are very good. Nice footwork at the sideline to make the most of tight spaces. Body is controlled and explosive enough to sell hesitations/double moves.
weaknesses: Comfortable in contested-catch situations but lacks size when getting the upper hand. Good burst and acceleration, but his long speed is lacking. Didn't show a good feel for sitting in soft spots versus zone. Could have been a QB issue.
bottom_line: Baker can be a solid WR3 for a vertical offense that likes to attack down the sidelines. His long-speed limitations hurt his ability to separate, but he is a competitive contested-catch receiver.

profile: Burton played two seasons at Georgia before transferring to Alabama, where he was a two-year starter, in 2022. He is a highly competitive wide receiver. He's not afraid of any matchup and will talk trash consistently. His quickness can be devastating, especially when paired with his ability to use a variety of releases. His long speed is smooth, but he appears to lack a rare final gear. However, he is still successful as a vertical receiver due to how strong he is at the catch point. His change-of-direction speed and flexibility allow him to run any route. If he can keep his cool, he can be an impact slot or flanker receiver in the NFL.
strengths: Versatile in his releases off the line of scrimmage. Nuanced player who understands winning in the "little" ways at the position. Can run the whole route tree, but he's mostly run vertical routes. Highly competitive player — constantly talking trash. Quick and violent hands versus press and when going up to catch passes.
weaknesses: Middling long speed could hamper how much cushion he is given from defenders at the next level. Smaller frame and smaller catch radius. Fiery player but can lose his temper. Has the competitiveness to be an impact blocker, just needs more consistency.
bottom_line: Burton brings a fiery approach to the position. As long as his size doesn't cause him to be pushed around, he has elite quickness to win against press and off coverage at the next level as a flanker or slot.

profile: Coker's production speaks for itself, but he also has good size and is above the 50th percentile in all measurables. He is a very smart receiver who understands how to win as a route runner. He'll hit defenders with head and shoulder fakes, as well as hand flashes and double moves to get open. He is always trying to maximize his catch radius with strong catches away from the body. His long speed is lacking and will be well below average in the NFL. Therefore, I am worried that he might not be big and fast enough to be an outside receiver but not quite quick enough to be a slot receiver.
strengths: Really nice body/speed control for a player whose height and weight rank above the 50th percentile. Nuanced route runner who can set defenders up with shoulder fakes, hand flashes and double moves. Consistent hands catcher who makes an effort to maximize catch radius away from his body.
weaknesses: Below-average long speed for the NFL. Might not have a home role in the NFL.
bottom_line: Coker's overall athleticism will have to be overcome, but he is a smart and versatile route runner who has reliable hands. He should be a draft-and-develop WR4/5 at the next level.

profile: Coleman originally committed to Michigan State as a two- sport athlete, and he transferred to Florida State in 2023. His evaluation is a test of how much scouts prefer contested- catch receivers to athletic separators. He is an impressive 6- foot-4 and 215-pound athlete who enjoys getting physical with cornerbacks, as he constantly catches passes through contact. While that yields jaw-dropping feats of strength, his lack of separation ability is concerning for the next level — there just aren't a lot of guys who make a living as consistent contested-catch receivers. The ones that do are often some of the best receivers in the league.
strengths: Very impressive athlete for a player his size. He is very explosive and strong. Some of the most impressive contested catches you'll see. Active, strong hands when he's lined up against press coverage.
weaknesses: Not a lot of lateral agility — if defenders get him going east-to -west, they can keep up with him. For as athletic as he is, not a big yards-after-catch receiver. Lack of separation is an issue. Contested catches are his strength, but every catch seems to be contested Limited route tree — basic vertical stem.
bottom_line: Coleman is a top-tier athlete for the position from an explosiveness standpoint. His burst, top speed and leaping ability are All-Pro caliber. However, the lack of agility in his game limits his route tree and ability to separate from defensive backs. Those who love above-the-rim (full pun intended), alpha- type receivers will be big fans, but his inability to consistently separate means he won't be for everyone.

profile: After two years as a running back at Western Kentucky, Corley found a home at receiver. He is a well-balanced athlete, which shows up in how he plays the position. That ball-carrier vision from his running back days has carried over. When he gets the ball in his hands, he immediately believes he's a running back again — in a good way. His contact balance and after-contact ability are impressive and consistent, as he is often utilized in the quick game. He also has some of the strongest hands in the class. However, his lack of receiver snaps has led to a limited route tree, a lack of releases and little nuance down the field.
strengths: Running back background shows up in contact balance and how he becomes a playmaker in yards-after-catch situations. Very strong hands to catch through contact. Good linear explosiveness when going in a straight line. Converts speed-to-power like a pass-rusher — he is tough to hit/bring down once he gets a full head of steam.
weaknesses: Lateral movements are a bit stiff when he gets up to speed. Not a very diverse route tree. Not much variation in his releases outside of a speed release. Struggles to get off contact against press coverage and at the contact point in his routes.
bottom_line: He is pretty raw in the nuances of playing receiver – release footwork, route tree and how to get off contact. Nonetheless, those are all things he can learn. If he does, he is a true weapon with the ball in his hands.

profile: Cowing has played a lot of football in his college career with over 3,000 snaps in his five-year college career. He has been a big volume receiver at UTEP and Arizona. His threat rate has not been below 25% for any season, and he had two seasons above 30%, showcasing how much both offenses wanted to get him the ball. He will truly be an outlier in his size — likely be below the fifth percentile in both height and weight— but the bottom line is he can win at the position.
strengths: Rapid acceleration given his size. Truly gifted route runner — he can create separation against any coverage or leverage. Great footwork when releasing off the line of scrimmage quickly and can get away from press coverage. Good yards-after-catch receiver if he has some daylight.
weaknesses: Size deficiencies make him an outlier. Not much of a strength profile to his game with yards after contact or contested catches. Too many drops over his career, even for the amount of targets he has seen.
bottom_line: If creating a separation window for your quarterback is the name of the game, not many, if any, do it better than Cowing. His role in the NFL will be niche in the slot, but there is a world where he can be a very productive player, as he has been his entire college football career.

profile: Franklin, a former four-star wide receiver recruit, played in all 14 games in his true freshman season at Oregon and started every game in his sophomore and junior seasons. He is a smooth strider as a vertical receiver. He was the top explosive-play pass catcher on Oregon's offense the past two seasons. His calling card is his ability as a vertical threat, both from the slot and the outside. Over the past two seasons, he diversified his releases and his general footwork to create separation in more ways than just through vertical speed. His play strength is a concern when fighting through the contact window and on contested catches.
strengths: Long, smooth strides that allow him to consistently threaten vertically Loaded pre-snap stance with no false steps, which allows him to quickly get to top speed Consistent hands catcher who extends his long arms for catches rather than let the ball into his body Really nice footwork that shows up in releases and ability to make players miss after the catch
weaknesses: Limited route tree. Basically just vertical routes (likely not due to lack of ability) General strength can be a concern, but it does not affect his willingness to go up strong for catches or get his nose into blocks
bottom_line: Franklin might get lost in the shuffle of a loaded wide receiver class, but he shouldn't. His smoothness comes from his athletic profile and his confidence in knowing how to win at the position. He needs to continue to get stronger but, overall, is a competitive player who can be a good WR2 for a vertical NFL offense.

profile: Gould brings a successful high school track background to the football field. Explosiveness and straight-line speed are his calling cards, allowing him to eat up cushions and put defenders in tough spots when he gets up to speed. He also has ample punt return experience, which will help as he looks to make an NFL roster. Though Gould is fast, he is small. His stature likely limits him to a slot-only role. He is a willing but ineffective run blocker. He also doesn't have the after-the- catch numbers one might expect for a player of his size, though his 81st-percentile average target depth shows that his college situation may have played a factor.
strengths: Brings experience and ability in the return game (mainly as a punt returner). Very fast player. Explosive in his first few steps and has impactful top speed.
weaknesses: Lacks the size and strength to compete at the catch point. Small catch radius. Willing but ineffective run blocker. Not a big yards-after-the-catch receiver.
bottom_line: Gould's speed will give him a shot in the NFL as a depth receiver and a special teams player. He projects as a slot-only player.

profile: Griffin received the nickname "Tulu" because he was always getting "too loose" when other teams chose to kick it to him in peewee and high school football. His speed and explosiveness are the focal points of his game, though he could stand to build more confidence in those traits before the catch. He possesses good enough straight-line speed and short-area explosiveness to be an effective route runner, but it's almost like he's holding back at times. He is not overly coordinated when catching the football, something that must improve if he wants to be more than just a return specialist in the NFL. He also needs to get stronger overall.
strengths: Good special teams experience, including return work. Good vertical receiver — you can tell he lets his speed loose when he is getting vertical. Has the athletic ability to be explosive in short areas. Turns into a different athlete once the ball gets in his hands. Has good change of direction and release combinations to get off press coverage.
weaknesses: Not as quick as he is explosive. His foot speed seems slow for his size when executing different releases and breaks. Catch technique and coordination can be clunky. Needs to attack the ball in the air more. Not as confident and explosive before the catch as he is after. Hands need to be more active against press coverage. Needs to be a stronger player overall.
bottom_line: Griffin will get drafted due to this kick and punt return ability. He has the athletic mold to be more of a flanker or slot, but he needs to be more consistent with his hands while diversifying his route tree to be more than just a "go" ball receiver.

profile: Harrison is one of the most complete prospects you will find. He displays an understanding of how to win at the position like few college players do. He is well beyond his years in his releases, his route tree and his IQ to set up and manipulate defenders when creating throwing windows. For a player as tall as he is (6-foot-4), his footwork, change of direction and long speed are excellent. He has very reliable hands and hand-eye coordination to make tough contested catches. One area where he could have stood to improve from 2022 was his after-the-catch ability, and he proved in 2023 that he can deliver in such situations.
strengths: Versatile in his releases off the line of scrimmage against press Body control is so good for a player of his size Active and precise hands to get off press Has the long speed to consistently threaten vertically Excellent hands. Makes the most of his catch radius and has spectacular catch ability and coordination Elite footwork. Release speed/cuts got even faster in ‘23 Willing blocker with good strength and long arms
weaknesses: Sometimes a little too much arm extension to push off to create separation (more of a 2022 concern) YAC speed is adequate but not elite
bottom_line: Harrison comes from Hall-of-Fame bloodlines, and you can see that in his tape without even knowing his last name. He has a truly rare blend of size, speed, strength and football IQ for such a young player. He will be a WR1-caliber player the day he is drafted, and one in the mold of a Tier 1 NFL wideout.

profile: Johnson is an experienced receiver prospect, having played 60 games with 44 starts at Michigan. He is a good overall athlete with a decent blend of straight-line speed, acceleration and change of direction. However, his change of direction can be a bit stiff, especially when he gets up to speed. He isn't an imposing blocker, but he is reliable in his positioning and fundamentals, which will help him make an NFL roster on special teams. His separation rates are very high, but that was more due to usage and setup than rare athletic ability. Johnson seems to have more in the tank talent-wise; we just didn't see it in his three years as a starter.
strengths: Excellent overall athlete. Good straight-line speed and burst with decent change of direction. Competitive player whether catching or blocking.
weaknesses: Not an imposing blocker, but a fundamental and reliable one. High separation rates are more due to setup and usage than rare athletic ability. Can be stiff when changing direction. Routes are more rounded than sharp.
bottom_line: Johnson seems more talented than his production suggests. His NFL role is likely that of a WR4 or WR5.

profile: Legette is a late bloomer. He was used mainly as a schemed- up yards-after-catch receiver in 2022 and was not trusted to win as a route runner. This past season was a much different story. Legette ascended to WR1 in South Carolina's offense and gave us a season of "wow" moments due to his athleticism while standing 6-foot-3 and 227 pounds. He has some of the most impressive contested catches of any receiver, and he can hit a top speed that most his size simply can't.
strengths: Impressive size-speed combination (hit over 22 miles per hour on a play in 2023). Dominant contested-catch receiver. Creates yards after the catch who can be emphasized in the quick game. Huge catch radius and makes the most of it — he made plenty of full extension receptions this season. Love his mentality to attack the ball in the air.
weaknesses: Not much variance in his releases and footwork off the line of scrimmage. Route tree is limited, but it feels like he can diversify it.
bottom_line: Legette does not have ample experience as the focal point of a passing attack, but 2023 showed he is capable of that. He is not as polished as a route runner/release-artist as he needs to be to achieve his potential at the NFL level, but teams take a chance on players of his build.

profile: McCaffrey is the son of Super Bowl champion receiver Ed McCaffrey and the brother of 49ers running back Christian McCaffrey. He doesn't have the same level of athleticism as Christian, but he is a highly nuanced receiver who maximizes his talent potential. He played quarterback for three years in college before moving to wide receiver. He is a savvy route runner — not just at the break point, but throughout his routes. He also has soft but strong hands to be a reliable target in all situations. McCaffrey is a good overall athlete but won't win off athleticism alone at the NFL level. He can also be pushed around a bit due to a lack of body density.
strengths: Very natural athlete who can go up and grab passes with fully extended arms. Nuanced route runner — not just in his cuts, but throughout the route. Impressive concentration and strength for contested catches. Fun potential as a passer for trick plays.
weaknesses: Good athlete, but lacks difference-making explosiveness to win off athleticism at the next level. Can get pushed around due to lack of body density. Struggles to create space against press due to lack of long speed.
bottom_line: McCaffrey is a big slot type of receiver with the route-running chops to make up for decent athleticism. His reliable hands in traffic make him a good depth receiver and a potential WR3 in the NFL.

profile: A three-star recruit with plenty of athletic versatility, McConkey played quarterback, running back, defensive back, punter and return specialist in high school. From his Georgia tape, McConkey is a highly nuanced receiver who has the athletic ability and football intelligence to be a difference- maker in the slot at the NFL level. His footwork and release variation give him the advantage against press coverage in the slot or on the outside. He also has good enough long speed to remain a threat vertically. He's on the smaller side, but that does not curb his willingness to be an impact blocker.
strengths: NFL-level quickness and acceleration out of his stance and breaks. He's a slot type of player, but he has notable long speed to go with outside receiver experience and ability. Impactful YAC receiver for the quick game Overall size affects his efficacy, but he is a very willing blocker with good fundamentals (they put him in condensed formations on short-yardage plays).
weaknesses: Releases have some false steps, but he is so quick and fast that it doesn't hurt his ability to be effective off the line. Limited catch radius for jump balls.
bottom_line: Don't expect McConkey to be an "X," jump ball receiver but outside of that, it's hard to imagine him not succeeding in the NFL. His game is reminiscent of Eddie Royal. Maybe not as fast with long speed, but he has devastating quickness, is good in the return game, and is a strong blocker for his size.

profile: McMillan was a four-star recruit out of high school and committed to Washington over offers from schools such as Notre Dame and Alabama. He proved to be a wide receiver craftsman with the Huskies. He shows a high level of receiver intelligence with his diverse route tree, feel for zone coverage and nuanced way of attacking defenders and their leverage. He is also strong at the catch point and lives for the big moments. He doesn't have rare change of direction or top speed, but he knows how to get open consistently in a variety of ways as a flanker or slot receiver.
strengths: Understands how to win with leverage and by attacking blind spots. Really good feel for finding soft spots against zone coverage. Fiesty and strong for a smaller receiver. Nuanced route runner who can run a variety of different routes in a fluid way. No wasted movement and explosive out of his releases.
weaknesses: Doesn't have an NFL top gear to be a consistent vertical threat and create vertical separation. Change of direction is good, not elite.
