bottom_line: McMillan was someone Washington continued to prioritize in their passing attack, even with players like Rome Odunze and Ja'Lynn Polk on the roster. His nuances give him a high floor as a WR2/3.

profile: Means is physically gifted in both strength and speed. His arm length, wingspan and hand size all rank above the 80th percentile, which plays into his game. He is at his best when he can get vertical, as his build-up speed is better than his short-area burst. His bigger frame makes short stop-and- start movements less effective. He also doesn't show a consistent feel for open space as an underneath receiver.
strengths: Huge wingspan and big hands are obvious pluses. Long arms can be an asset in blocking as well. Physically gifted player with both strength and speed.
weaknesses: Doesn't show the best "feel" for the space when running routes and gaining yards after the catch. Bigger body takes longer to stop and change direction. Long speed is better than his acceleration. Has the physical profile to be a good blocker but lacks consistency in technique and competitiveness.
bottom_line: Means is a vertical receiver who has a good physical profile for a streamlined role (fast, strong, big catch radius for contest opportunities deep). He can be a depth WR4/5 for a team that likes to push the ball vertically consistently.

profile: Mitchell began his career at Georgia, where he won back-to- back national championships. In 2023, he transferred to Texas to be closer to his daughter. He is an alluring outside receiver. At 6-foot-4, he has more finesse than most bigger- bodied receivers — his releases are quick, his change of direction is fluid and his acceleration is smooth. His skill set puts a ton of stress on cornerbacks. He could attack the ball with more intensity, and his presence can be inconsistent, but he brings starting NFL ability to the table. He was a touchdown machine for Texas and Georgia, reaching the end zone 14 times across 18 starts over the past two seasons.
strengths: Fast, fluid route runner for his size. Fast footwork for quick releases off the line. Effective shoulder dip when running by defenders. Understands the nuance of how to get open, especially deep.
weaknesses: The shoulder dip to avoid contact in his route is good, but he needs to be more willing to chop defenders' hands away as well. Release speed is fast, but there are some false and wasted steps. He could do a better job of attacking the ball in the air. His body language and effort can be very different when he’s a primary receiver versus when he's not.
bottom_line: Mitchell's fluidity at his size makes him a tough matchup, especially in the red zone. The biggest area of concern I have with him is that I wish he attacked the ball more when it was in the air. If he improves in that category, he has fringe WR1/WR2 abilities.

profile: It does not take long when watching Nabers' tape to see that he moves differently compared to even the best in college football. His ability to accelerate while changing direction gives him a very high ceiling as a separation specialist. Though the strength elements of the position are a bit of a concern, his feet are lightning-quick to get off press at the line of scrimmage. He could stand to be more aggressive at the catch point (fewer body catches), but if that and his catching through contact improve, he has everything else to be a very dangerous NFL receiver.
strengths: Short-area explosiveness and control remind of an elite CB Footwork is lightning quick. He can get defenders turned around immediately off the snap Elite separation athleticism. Acceleration ability while changing direction is rare Is a consistent vertical threat from the outside or the slot
weaknesses: Hands are too low at the snap and when getting into his route. He will often lose first contact because of it Could add even more nuance/manipulation in his routes. Relies on elite change-of-direction ability right now. Will be unstoppable if he can attack leverage/manipulate coverage with more subtlety Could attack the ball better in the air. Lets it come into his body too often
bottom_line: Nabers' movement skills are rare, even at the NFL level. His ability to change direction yet continue to accelerate makes him an open-target specialist in the slot and on the outside. He has the kind of athleticism that demands a defense to know where he is at all times as a future WR1.

profile: Odunze, a former four-star recruit, was named the Nevada Gatorade Player of the Year in 2019. In addition to his football success, he won a state title in the 200-meter dash. His Washington tape is that of an alluring receiver prospect, one whose build and ability do not come around often. He checks the boxes for height, weight and arm length to play all three receiver positions. He does the same from an athletic standpoint. His route running is smooth for a player of his size, and his acceleration is equally impressive. He became a more reliable pass catcher through contact in 2023 and is comfortable hauling in throws away from his body.
strengths: Excellent hands. Has a large catch radius and can fully extend for catches through contact Impressive ability to change speeds at his size and weight Good vertical ability. Has a nice final top gear to separate Versatile route runner who can execute simple and complex routes Reliable, willing blocker
weaknesses: Little slower to flip his hips on comeback routes, but nothing glaring when taking into account his size Not a lot of yards after the catch, but that is likely more due to ball placement/routes than a lack of playmaking ability Hands are low in his release setup, which can make it easier for press defenders to get hands on him
bottom_line: In an offense filled with future NFL players at the skill positions, Odunze was the best of the bunch. If he weren't in a class with Marvin Harrison Jr. and Malik Nabers, we would be talking about him as an easy WR1 and a player worthy of a top-10 pick, although the latter is still true for 2024.

profile: Pearsall, a three-star recruit, also played safety in high school. He started his career at Arizona State before transferring to Florida in 2022. He is a projected slot receiver, and his slot skill set is about as good as one could hope. He is savvy and nuanced in his route running, winning in so many ways with a diverse route tree. His feet are quick and elusive, which allows him to be more of a vertical threat than his straight-line speed alone could create. He is also a very reliable hands catcher. He doesn't have rare flexibility for change of direction, but he makes up for it with how he sets up defenders.
strengths: Nuanced and savvy route runner — always uses head/shoulder fake to create a little bit more separation. Quick off the line with good releases. Tough receiver who has some great receptions through contact.
weaknesses: Agility is a bit stiff for a player of his size with his projected role. Was a decent vertical threat at the college level but likely won’t be based off straight-line speed in the NFL — scheme could help him.
bottom_line: Ultimately, Pearsall won't intimidate defenders on the line of scrimmage, but he will once the ball is snapped. He is a ready- made slot receiver who can contribute early in his NFL career.

profile: Polk has been a productive receiver since his high school days, stacking up with Dez Bryant and Keke Coutee on his high school's receiving records. He is a highly competitive player who will earn his spot on an NFL roster through tough catches, reliable hands and a willingness to be physical. He has shorter strides, which causes a lack of true top-gear speed, but his strides are explosive. His upright stance and low hands at the snaps might cause some issues getting off press coverage at the next level. Despite the lack of top gear, he can be an impactful vertical receiver due to how comfortable he is playing through contact.
strengths: Reliable hands catcher — catches through contact well. Hands are active to fight off defenders at contact in press or when getting vertical. Willing blocker on run plays — does not take plays off. Good short-area explosiveness — nice acceleration off the line and at the breakpoint.
weaknesses: Shorter stride length doesn't yield a fast top gear of speed for separation. Rounds his route more than true breaks. Narrow base out of his stance makes it more challenging to generate power and leverage to get off press. Hands are low in his stance, giving up his chest for press defenders to dictate contact.
bottom_line: Polk is a limited route runner, but he is also one of the best "go up and get it" contested catch receivers in this class (and that is really saying something). His knack for making big plays should always get him on an NFL roster in some capacity.

profile: As the son of the most accomplished receiver in NFL history, Rice's football intelligence sets him apart from most of his peers. There is so much nuance to how he plays the position — much more than you'd expect, even for the more polished receiver prospects. He has a vast understanding of releases, route running and hand techniques. He is a smooth runner who can gain separation at all three levels of the field. He isn't the most dynamic athlete, so his NFL Combine testing will be big for his draft stock. He also brings special teams experience as a returner.
strengths: Long strides make for decent long speed (former track sprinter). Very intelligent route runner. Impressive blocker — fundamentally sound and does not give up on blocks quickly. Long arms help with dictating and maintaining blocks. Active hands against press and tight coverage.
weaknesses: Change of direction is more smooth than sudden. Long speed is adequate but doesn't appear to have a rare top gear.
bottom_line: Rice's name will come with high expectations but in terms of how he plays the position, his ability to win as a route runner is better than most of the receivers in this class. His high football intelligence should enable him to be a high-floor player in the NFL.

profile: Robinson is an explosive slot receiver who has decent nuance in his routes to create separation. His footwork is quick and explosive off the line of scrimmage with good potential for effective releases. Robinson is still working on his feel for being open when running through zone coverages. It is tough for him to get open once defenders get their hands on him. He has the body control to make good adjustments to the ball and decent strength for contested catches, but both are inconsistent. He had a drop issue in 2023. As a blocker, he is willing and fast to his keys but can often overshoot or fail to line them up properly.
strengths: Quick, controlled and explosive athlete. Explosive footwork to get out of his stance. Good overall athleticism and body control. Has some nice nuance in his route by veering one way and exploding another. Decent strength for contested catches.
weaknesses: Overaggressive when setting players up for blocks — gets there quickly but can overshoot defenders. Six drops in 2023. Long speed is limited (but he's a slot, so that's OK). Still developing a feel for getting open when running crossing routes through zones. Struggles to create space after defenders get their hands on him.
bottom_line: Robinson is an NFL-caliber athlete for a slot receiver, but he is a very inconsistent player in a handful of categories. He is a nice draft-and-develop option for Day 3.

profile: Rosemy-Jacksaint's first college score ended in disaster — a gruesome broken leg that sidelined him for 10 months. He then struggled to find consistent playing time at Georgia and didn't become a regular starter until his senior season, but that 2023 tape showed an effective player. He understands the nuances and angles of route running, and his technique allows him to execute comeback routes with precision. He also has some of the most reliable hands in the class, rarely letting the ball come into his body. He takes pride in blocking and special teams work. Unfortunately, he is without an NFL- level top gear and struggles to separate.
strengths: Conscious with his hand usage to get off press coverage. Fundamentally sound in how he chops his feet and flips his hips for comeback routes. Long legs, long arms. Consistently gets the ball in the air. Not the strongest blocker due to size, but he takes pride in it. Great hands — Zero drops on 93 targets over the last two years. Intelligent player who understands nuances of route running, attacking leverage, boxing out for catches, etc.
weaknesses: Doesn't have an NFL-level top gear. Lacks the twitch and explosiveness to create separation. Lacks the strength to create consistent separation with contact. Has a tough time getting off jams in versus press.
bottom_line: Rosemy-Jacksaint lacks difference-making NFL athleticism, but he is a determined, intelligent player who can round out a receiver room with special teams experience to boot. Expect him to be a priority Day 3 depth player.

profile: Across more than 2,100 snaps in his college career, Smith played as a receiver, running back and punt returner for Texas A&M. His short-area explosiveness is better than his long speed, but that long speed should be enough for the NFL. He is always trying to set up defenders with head fakes, shoulder shimmies and hard cuts on his routes. He also brings a variety of releases with a good understanding of why and how they work. He won't be a jump-ball, contested-catch receiver, but his competitiveness can't be questioned. He was asked to block the likes of Chris Braswell and Harold Perkins but didn't back down.
strengths: Consistent as a returner. Conscious suddenness to his game. Change of direction acceleration is above average. RB experience shows up immediately when he gets the ball. Variety of releases with a good understanding of why and how they work. Highly competitive player. Was asked to block the likes of Chris Braswell and Harold Perkins but didn't back down.
weaknesses: A little stiff to truly change direction when running near full speed but at slower speeds, he can really flip the hips. Long speed may be average at best, so testing will be big for him there. Won't be a jump ball type of receiver. Short arms lend to a shorter catch radius.
bottom_line: For teams looking for an underneath slot receiver who wins with suddenness, savviness and blocking while contributing on special teams, Smith will be a name on their list. That likely yields Day 2 value on draft weekend.

profile: Thomas is the kind of player every offense wants for their vertical passing game plans. As a former football and basketball star in high school, he is a big, tall and fast vertical threat who demands the defense to always be honest about his ability to get behind them. His footwork and flexibility are fast and fluid for a big man. From 2022-2023, his releases became more effective in creating separation. He is also a willing and competitive blocker. He posted a career-high catch percentage in 2023, and that needs to continue moving forward.
strengths: Smooth, long strides with good top speed to consistently threaten vertically Much-improved technique and footwork on his releases in 2023 Willing and competitive blocker
weaknesses: Not a lot of experience versus press Catch percentage was lower than preferred the past three years (though 2023 was his best) Not a "make you miss" type of receiver after the catch
bottom_line: Thomas offers a good combination of size and speed to push the ball vertically down the sideline, demanding safeties stay rotated to his side. To truly unlock that kind of threat, he will need to show he can consistently beat press coverage. Offenses that like to push the ball will prioritize what he brings to the table in the top 50.

profile: Thrash's college football journey began at Georgia State, where he now ranks fifth in team history in receiving yards (1,752), eighth in receptions (104) and tied for sixth in touchdown receptions (12). Thrash is a smooth vertical threat with a good understanding of angles and leverage to attack all sorts of coverage deployments. He has very nice separation scores, but he's not as explosive as some of his peers. Rather than win with twitch, he wins with nuance and subtleties, which is an art, given how often he plays near the sideline. He needs to improve his hands after dropping 16 passes over the past three seasons.
strengths: Runs route with nuance — good manipulation of a defensive back's leverage and blind spot. Good all-around athlete — adequate levels of long speed, agility and acceleration. Pretty strong at the catch point.
weaknesses: Eight drops in 2023 for a sub-90% catchable passes reception percentage — 16 dropped passes over the last three seasons. Smoother speed rather than true explosive acceleration.
bottom_line: Thrash is a good all-around athlete who has a knack for setting defenders up to create subtle separation near the sideline. His combine scores will be important for him to stand out in a stacked receiver class.

profile: Walker has the makings of a game-changing NFL receiver. When he was at Kent State in 2022, he played against Washington, Oklahoma and Georgia to start the season and not only looked like he belonged but was the best player on the field, at times. He is incredibly explosive. He consistently catches with his hands and can snag grabs through contact. In 2023, his footwork wasn't as precise, but he was much better in 2022. His route running right now is based on him winning vertically. He needs to be more nuanced, diverse and precise if he wants to consistently get by NFL cornerbacks.
strengths: Active hands on the line of scrimmage — uses both his hands and feet to effectively get off press coverage. Very impressive athlete who has NFL-level explosiveness and top speed. Hands catcher who understands the importance of extension. Strong contested-catch player.
weaknesses: In 2023, his route running was not as crisp. He needs more refinement, but we saw that in 2022. 2023 did not show a polished player (again, 2022 did more). Limited snaps against legitimate competition.
bottom_line: Walker is not a polished product, but at 6-foot-2 and 200 pounds, he has the footspeed and vertical ability to put a lot of stress on a defense to cover deep. Overall, this is an NFL athlete who has even more room to improve and has the potential to get picked in the top 60.

profile: Washington was one of the most productive players in the country in 2023. He's small, and that has its disadvantages — he lacks natural strength and length for jump balls and blocking assignments. Nonetheless, his footwork is precise and sudden, which makes him an effective separation player from the slot, especially when finding soft spots in zone coverage. He has an excellent first step to chew up a defensive back's cushion. He also has an above-average ability to change direction yet maintain or regain speed. He does not have much experience against press coverage, so he is likely a slot-only receiver.
strengths: Compact build with good strength/balance. Quick, controlled feet make for precise cuts and good suddenness. Consistently extends hands to the catch point. He has strong hands, too.
weaknesses: Short arms make for a shorter catch radius. Shorter arms make it tougher for him to be an effective blocker against longer corners. Limited long speed. Will be tough for him to have a depth/special teams role with how ineffective he can be at blocking.
bottom_line: Washington is a tough assignment in the slot due to how fast he accelerates and his ability to create separation with quick changes of direction. He is a slot-only type of receiver due to his lack of size and strength, but he is tough to cover.

profile: Washington is a smaller receiver who projects to a slot/special teams role at the next level. He grew up as a multi-sport athlete, playing soccer and football in high school while also running/jumping on the track team. He brings that all-around athletic ability to the football field in a variety of ways. USC lined him up in the backfield, in the slot and even as an H-back, at times. He is a strong hands catcher and was his best in that area in 2023. Despite his size, he does not have elite change-of-direction ability or vertical speed.
strengths: Smooth shoulder dip when running past defenders in shallow zones. Strong hands catcher, especially in 2023. Has ample special teams experience over the past two seasons. USC used him all over; slot, flanker, H-back, running back.
weaknesses: Makes Jordan Addison look big. Does not have the Tank-Dell-like change-of-direction ability for a player of similar size. Very limited experience and effectiveness versus press (slot-only type). Willing blocker but not an effective one.
bottom_line: Washington's size will likely limit his playing time at the next level, but he could be an ideal WR4/5 as a nice depth piece and slot receiver on offense in addition to a return man/punt coverage gunner on special teams.

profile: Much of Whittington's college career was hampered by injuries: a torn groin his first year, a torn meniscus his second year and a broken clavicle his third year. He stayed healthy the past two seasons, and when on the field, he showed he's an all-around, balanced athlete. Unfortunately, it does appear injuries have impacted his explosiveness vertically and laterally, but they haven't taken away all of his ability. His best work comes from the slot, where he can create throwing windows that allow him to gain yards after the catch.
strengths: Explosive and athletic posture in his pre-snap stance, which allows him to generate a ton of power in his first step. Willing blocker. Good yards-after-contact kind of player (RB background).
weaknesses: Stiff in his lateral movements when running routes — limited route tree. Limited long speed to threaten vertically and create separation with speed. Willing blocker but a little inconsistent.
bottom_line: He projects as a slot receiver at the NFL level, one with a thicker build for yards after the catch and contact. Unfortunately, he has an extensive injury history, which may go into his limited athletic profile when stacked up against players at the NFL level. Nonetheless, he has been healthy the last two seasons and can be a versatile depth player at the next level.

profile: Williams' scouting report starts with his devastating quickness. He is explosive and controlled in his movements, especially in his releases off the line of scrimmage. He can also change up his release speed to put cornerbacks in tough spots. His explosiveness allows him to create separation without contact and even through contact. He has great body control to make tough adjustments for catches. Williams' lack of size affects both his blocking and tackle-breaking potential, and his shorter arms and smaller hands limit his catch radius.
strengths: Releases are precise. Knows how to stop quickly and create separation after defenders get hands on him. Very impressive body control for acrobatic catches and in-air adjustments. Quick acceleration but limited long speed.
weaknesses: Feisty but won’t be a blocking weapon, given his size. Contested catches can be there but are tough with his size. Limited catch radius with smaller arms and hands. Has a tough time breaking tackles. Isn't as much of a "make you miss" playmaker as he could be after the catch.
bottom_line: Williams is a specific type of small slot receiver, but one whose quickness can make him a tough speed matchup against slower nickel defenders. He has WR4/5 potential.

profile: Wilson is a very intriguing prospect due to his coordination and athleticism for his size (both height and weight). He doesn't show a lack of balance, poor footwork or a lack of fluidity — even his change of direction is good relative to his size. He has a massive catch radius, which he has used often to his advantage. But his hands — both with and without contact — need to be more reliable. If he can show more fire and focus at the catch point, he can be an impactful receiver, especially in the red zone.
strengths: Size is obviously a massive advantage for him. Pterodactyl catch radius. Much more coordinated, balanced and explosive than most receivers who measure in above 6-foot-6. Typically catches the ball with extended hands away from the body. Where agility is compromised due to size, he does have nice acceleration out of breaks.
weaknesses: Has some frustrating drops. Could stand to attack the ball in the air with more determination. Needs better hand placement as a blocker. Hand usage could be better when working off contact early contact/press and trying to create a separation at the catch point. Has some expected lack of wiggle/change-of-direction flexibility due to his size, but for his size, it's actually not bad at all.
bottom_line: It's hard to watch Wilson's tape and not be intrigued enough to take him at the back end of Day 2. He has some frustrating drops, but there is so much more to like, which is rooted in how well he moves for a player of his size.

profile: Wilson was born with speed in his DNA. His mother was a track star in high school, setting school and state records. Wilson himself ran a 4.37-second 40-yard dash in high school. So it goes without saying he is one of the class' fastest receivers. Before he became a full-time starter, Michigan used him to stretch the field. He earned a receiver threat rate of over 20% in three consecutive seasons. Defenses have to pay attention to him when he is on the field. Despite his small size, he brings good strength as a receiver and a blocker. He's not as agile as he is explosive but still projects well in a slot role for a vertical passing attack.
strengths: Gets upfield very quickly via athleticism and no wasted movement out of his stance. Effective vertical speed. Willing and strong blocker. Expanded release repertoire in 2023. Reliable hands catcher, even through contact.
weaknesses: Lateral movements are not as impressive as linear movements. Short catch radius. Difficulty getting off contact when he gets downfield.
bottom_line: In a different receiver class, Wilson would be much higher on these rankings. He not only brings NFL-level speed but also NFL-level determination at the catch point and when blocking. His tape shows a player coaches would love to have.

profile: Worthy has difference-making NFL speed. He got off to a hot start at Texas, owning about every freshman receiving record in the Longhorns' record book. He's not just a straight-line sprinter — his footwork, acceleration, one-cut burst and vertical speed must be accounted for on every play. However, his play strength is a concern, as he does not fight off contact well and can get locked up against press coverage.
strengths: Functional NFL speed, not just a straight-line sprinter. He can vary his speeds to still be an efficient route runner while operating at high speeds. Elite vertical threat. Elite explosiveness and acceleration when changing direction. Good deep tracking ability — can adjust when ball placement goes awry. Lightning quick footwork when releasing off the LOS.
weaknesses: Struggles to separate again physical coverage. Can get locked up against good press corner who gets their hands on him early (got locked up by Tre'Vius Hodges-Tomlinson). Does not use his hands to fight off defenders when he attempts to run by them vertically. Strength is a consistent concern with his game, especially in regards to his catch reliability.
bottom_line: Worthy must be identified pre-snap in all situations due to how easily he can take a pass to the house if not accounted for. If he can get stronger and learn to be a better hand fighter with defenders, he can be an impact pass catcher as a WR2/3.

profile: All is an all-around tight end prospect. He is a willing move blocker who is often detached from the line of scrimmage to lead, get to the second level or perform split-zone blocking responsibilities. He brings blocking fundamentals and good hand usage, though he could display more of a finisher's mentality. He understands how to use leverage and angles to wall off defenders without holding. He has big hands, although he did have frustrating drops in college. All is a better athlete than he gets credit for, as his change-of- direction fluidity yielded high separation rates in 2023. He also showcases good balance for yards after the catch.
strengths: Willing blocker with a good understanding of leverage and angles to wall players off without holding. Conscious hand usage and placement to initiate and hold blocks. Functional movement skills for blocking and receiving. Has nice change of direction. Able to flip his hips well for a big receiver (high separation rates). Big hands that measure above 10 inches.
weaknesses: Routes can look slow at times, but that doesn't stem from a lack of explosiveness — just inconsistency. Could use more nastiness when blocking. He has shown it, so we know it's there. Limited game action over the past two years due to injury.
bottom_line: All could use a bit more nastiness in his game, but this is a player with a versatile, contributing skill set who projects as a TE2 at the next level if he can stay healthy.

profile: Barner has been a late bloomer throughout his football career, culminating in a career year in 2023. In 2022, he was slow off the line of scrimmage and in his routes. This past season showed a quicker, more explosive version of himself, though one that is still below average for the NFL. His calling card is blocking. His best work comes from an inline or wingback position, where he can push people around. He takes pride in his blocking, as he's constantly looking for work and has excellent grip and core strength to maintain blocks. He can erase secondary players near the line of scrimmage, and he can even push defensive ends around, at times.
strengths: Strong blocker. Has the grip and core strength to maintain blocks and wall defenders off. Height and strength make high-pointing passes one of his strengths as a receiver. Impactful split-zone blocker. Improved release speed and versatility in 2023.
weaknesses: Below-average athlete in all facets. Very slow to change direction in his routes.
bottom_line: Though Barner won't give you much in the receiving game, he is an ideal TE2/3 for a team that likes to run heavy formations.

profile: Bell is a "tweener" for the tight end position but brings versatility as an offensive weapon with experience at inline tight end, wingback, running back and wide receiver. He has solid overall athleticism, with top speed and balance being his best traits. While his routes are good for a tight end, they are still rounded and don't create much separation against single coverage. He is also still finding a feel for zone coverage, too often simply running his route instead of speeding up or slowing down for space. Bell brings nice pop at contact as a blocker but does not maintain blocks consistently.
strengths: Versatile football background. Played receiver in high school and running back in college, in addition to tight end. Can be a legit receiving option as a wingback, fullback or running back. Good vision for space as a RB and yards-after-the-catch receiver. Good balance for yards after contact. Hands are 10-plus inches.
weaknesses: Size puts him in between positions. Smaller for a tight end, big for a running back. Brings pop at contact when blocking but doesn't maintain blocks well. Doesn't always have the best feel for zone coverage.
bottom_line: Bell is an easy roster depth piece because of how many roles he can play, but he needs to find a better feel for zone coverage as a receiver and must maintain blocks better.

profile: Bowers is one of the most well-rounded tight end prospects to ever enter the NFL. At Georgia, he was the SEC's Freshman of the Year. In both his sophomore and junior seasons, he was an All-American and the John Mackey Award winner (nation's top tight end). His build-up speed is good for the NFL, which is why he has elite after-the-catch ability. He has some of the strongest hands you'll see for a tight end. As a blocker, he might be the strongest pound-for-pound tight end you'll find. His versatility allows him to be an elite pre-snap movement piece, as defenses have to account for where he is at all times and in all formations.
strengths: Even (and extensive) snap experience between inline and slot — ultimate chess piece as a pre-snap motion player. Pound for pound a powerful and reliable run blocker — great lead blocker on split zone concepts and counters. Blocking ability in space is fundamentally sound and reliable. Impressive after-catch ability due to his balance and yards after contact. He’s also a contested-catch machine. Change of direction is solid. Good build-up top speed.
weaknesses: A little stiff when it comes to cuts in his routes — this explains his low separation percentage against single coverage. Route tree could be somewhat limited. Build up speed rather than twitched explosiveness, but the build- up is fast.
bottom_line: Outside of being on the smaller side, Bowers is a dream tight end prospect who can be an impact player in the slot, out wide and inline. Add in his reliable blocking ability on the line and in space, and you have an ultimate chess piece offensive weapon with All-Pro potential.

profile: Holker will be one of the older prospects in the class. He started his football career at BYU and transferred to Colorado State in 2023. Though smaller for the position, listed at 6- foot-4 and 235 pounds, he is a well-rounded athlete. He has a good first step and decent build-up speed to be a consistent vertical threat, especially over the middle. He displays strong hands for making contested catches over the middle. He isn't a twitched-up athlete, so his routes are very rounded, which affects his separation potential. While he is a patient and fundamentally sound blocker, his lack of weight shows up against bigger front-seven players.
strengths: Natural mover — not an elite athlete but is a well-rounded one. Conscious to always attack defenders square between the shoulders when blocking. Has some tough catches up the seam and over the middle
weaknesses: Lack of twitch and change-of-direction flexibility limits his route- running ability. Routes breaks are very rounded rather than hard cuts. Fundamentally sound blocker but not an imposing one (lower weight profile goes into that)
bottom_line: Holker is a well-rounded, versatile tight end who can be a good depth piece to pay in multi-tight end offenses, but he likely lacks the top-tier athleticism to be a TE1.

profile: Johnson brings plus size to the tight end position, ranking above the 70th percentile in height and weight. His long arms are an advantage when he is blocking edge rushers and hauling in passes. He has decent build-up and long speed when getting vertical up the seam, but he lacks the difference-making change-of-direction ability, which limits his route tree. He makes his money from an inline spot as a versatile blocker and pass catcher in heavier formations. He is a strong blocker when he targets defenders between the shoulders, but he can sometimes get crossed up (another area where his limited lateral ability shows).
strengths: Arm length is a big plus when blocking — can match up length- wise with edge players and outreach defensive backs. Size is a big plus for him — big catch radius due to his long arms. Decent build-up and top speed for a player of his size. Built for in-line play.
weaknesses: Lateral movements and change of direction are below average due to size. Lack of change of direction flexibility limits route tree.
bottom_line: Johnson brings alluring size to the position with plus length for blocking and when hauling in passes. He is a developmental tight end who shows runs good vertical routes and thrives when blocking, but he needs to be more consistent in both areas.

profile: McLachlan played wide receiver in high school back in Alberta, Canada, and that receiver background is evident in his tape. He will likely be a big slot receiver at the next level due to a lack of weight/blocking profile. He cannot be an inline tight end in his current state due to inconsistencies as a blocker. His acceleration and top speed are smooth and impressive for a player of his size. He also turns into a good playmaker after the catch with a mentality for extra yards through speed or contact.
strengths: Smooth athlete for his size. Impressive acceleration to generate yards after the catch. Turns into a playmaker after the catch.
weaknesses: Blocking consistency is lacking from fundamentals to power. Head dips and confidence fades when approaching blocks. Short arms despite being taller.
bottom_line: McLachlan is a good athlete for his size to get an opportunity as a big slot receiver, but his lack of blocking profile makes him a liability inline in his current state.

profile: Reiman has the body of an NFL tight end. He was a zero-star recruit who played both linebacker and tight end in high school and opted to walk on to Illinois as a tight end. He is well above the 50th percentile in size, but he carries it well. Reiman can push people as a run blocker, but he struggles to line guys up and has a bad tendency to lunge when blocking in space. His feet, hands and balance are all reliable in pass protection. While he doesn't have the suddenness for a diverse route tree/heavy usage in the passing game, his explosiveness can make him a good vertical option in heavy- tight end formations.
strengths: A linear athlete who moves well for his size despite subpar change of direction. Has the strength to sled-push defenders when he gets them between his shoulders. Brings necessary straight-line build-up speed to be a vertical option. Impressive grip strength and balance for sustained blocks in pass protection.
weaknesses: Is often not square and instead lunges to block in space. Likely not sudden enough in change of direction to be more than a heavy-personnel secondary tight end. Not as reliable in contested-catch situations as expected.
bottom_line: Reiman is a throwback tight end with size and physicality. He is limited as a lateral athlete but has the potential to be a TE2 in an NFL offense that likes bigger tight ends.

profile: Sanders, a former five-star recruit, looks like a super-sized athlete. Coming mostly from an inline or wing-back position, he is a constant vertical threat and a mismatch for most linebackers in coverage. His hands are reliable, as he did not drop a single pass in 2023. His explosive movement skills allow him to run routes like a receiver. If he wasn't on a team that also included Adonai Mitchell, Xavier Worthy and Jordan Whittington, he could've easily been a 1,000-yard receiver. He possesses all the tools to be an impact blocker, as well. His tape does include snaps where he lacks the necessary blocking physicality against smaller players.
strengths: True athlete for the position, as his long speed, acceleration and change of direction are all All-Pro caliber. He moves like a giant wide receiver — can run any route. Has the intangibles to be a good blocker but just isn't physical enough at times. A lot of his snaps came from inline, which made him a very tough seam and vertical matchup for defenses.
weaknesses: I wish he approached blocking with more violence (did improve in 2023). Still a bit clunky with some of the nuances for the position (footwork as a split zone blocker, lining up defenders in space).
bottom_line: Sanders is a Tier 1 athlete for the tight end position. He is still mastering the nuances of tight end play, and he needs more of a mean streak consistently as a blocker. However, even with those concerns, what he brings to the table as a vertical threat is worth a top-50 pick.

profile: Sinnott chose to go the walk-on route at Kansas State after playing defensive end and tight end in high school. He was one of the team's most versatile players over the past two years, lining up in the backfield, inline and in the slot. He is quick, which is not an adjective used often for tight ends. His foot speed allows him to accelerate and speedily change directions. While he is a willing blocker, defensive ends can overpower him. He is tough at the catch point but has shorter arms, which hinders his catching ability. His catch rate could also be higher. One would think he could excel on special teams, but he does not have that experience.
strengths: Quick athlete, which is not common for tight ends. Versatile movement skills that allow him to be effective in the slot, inline and out of the backfield. Fast split-zone and lead blocker. Not the strongest but a willing blocker.
weaknesses: Can get overpowered somewhat easily by bigger defensive ends. Hands are fine but not a major plus. Struggles to get off press coverage. Seems to have shorter arms, which shows up at the catch point and when blocking longer pass-rushers. Surprisingly lacks special teams experience.
bottom_line: Sinnot is a true jack-of-all-trades tight end who can line up in the backfield, on the line of scrimmage and at reciever. His game lacks a true trump card, but he's the type of football player every NFL team wants in their tight end room as a versatile role player.

profile: Spann-Ford is a massive tight end prospect who was a two- year starter for Minnesota. His size can be overwhelming for defensive backs to cover when he is off the line of scrimmage. However, he doesn't move in a way where he can be relied upon there often. He has the build of an inline tight end, but his blocking remains inconsistent. He will go for crushing blocks and whiff quicker defenders too often. He doesn't doesn't pack as much of a punch at contact as you would expect.
strengths: Big, imposing frame. Large catch radius. When he gets to the second level, he can overwhelm some lighter linebackers and defensive backs when blocking.
weaknesses: Size should make blocking his calling card, but he is not as physical as he needs to be. Does not pack a punch on contact for blocking. Goes for big blocks too often, which yields whiffs.
bottom_line: Spann-Ford's unique size will be his biggest asset to making an NFL roster, but his game right now is of a depth or practice squad player.

profile: Stover flip-flopped between linebacker and tight end at Ohio State, so it's clear he is a versatile athlete. He has a great build with good body control and balance, which shows up particularly when blocking. He is an intelligent blocker with patience and strength for his size. In the receiving game, he has reliable strong hands for contested catches. He shows good burst out of his stance, but his long speed will not be a major difference-maker at the next level. His intelligence allows him to run a diverse route tree, but his lack of lateral flexibility and explosiveness limits his separation ability beyond vertical routes.
strengths: First step is adequate to get upfield and create some space — you can see the DE background in how he fires off his front foot. Actually has some nice nuance in his routes with hand fighting, tempo and shoulder/head fakes. High blocking intelligence — lining guys up in space, hand placement, etc. He’s reliable and impactful in run blocking. Nice balance through contact. Strong and reliable hands (2 drops on 100+ targets in 2022-23).
weaknesses: Route tree is pretty diverse, but separation via lateral movements won't be one of his strengths. Won't win with top speed at the next level.
bottom_line: Stover is a well-rounded, well-versed football player whose natural athletic ability and fundamentally sound approach to the position should make him a high-floor role player with TE1 potential.

profile: Wiley really was not used in the passing offense until this past year but showed that his best could be ahead of him. Being a tight end at the NFL level can be more demanding than people realize. You have to have a rare blend of size and movement skills that most humans don't have. Wiley has that combination. He maximizes his catch radius and has an extremely low drop rate. His route tree is limited by the number of routes he ran, but he has the natural athleticism to be a decent route runner. He needs to improve both his finishing mentality and footwork in blocking for better consistency.
strengths: Ideal blend of size and natural athleticism for the position. When he gets a defender between the shoulder pads, he has the ability to really lock onto blocks. Can be an effective blocker against linebackers and defensive backs in space. Comfortable maximizing his catch radius for throws away from his body. Explosive getting out of his stance.
weaknesses: Feet can be slow in blocking at times. Wish there was a bit more fire for finishing blocks.
bottom_line: Wiley has an ideal size/athleticism combination to be a contributing TE2/3 at the next level.

profile: He is well-built with good height, weight and length, especially for a guard. At tackle this past season, he showed why he likely won't stick there at the NFL level. His hand placement is far too inconsistent to be on an island on the outside, and he is overaggressive while exposing his inside shoulder during pass sets. He has good leg drive and finishing ability in the run game, and his movement skill likely translates best to zone-blocking concepts.
strengths: Well-built guard prospect who has good mobility to boot. Has decent leg drive to move defenders when he hits them between the shoulder pads. Impressive mirror ability (though inconsistent with anticipation).
weaknesses: Misses on his target acquisition, which is why many worry about him on an island at offensive tackle. High out of his stance — lacks flexibility to really sit and get low. Overaggressive on his pass sets. He just does not have a good feel for staying in front of defenders as a tackle (moving to guard will help). He doesn't really use his length to his advantage consistently.
bottom_line: Adams is still a developmental guard prospect. Moving to guard will mitigate some of his biggest issues, as he has the size and movement skills to be a potential starter in a zone-blocking scheme.

profile: Alt is an easy first-round offensive lineman on film, bringing a high football IQ at just 21 years old. He started as a true freshman at Notre Dame, playing more than 2,200 snaps in his three-year career. Despite being 6-foot-8, he has good flexibility to get in a three-point stance in run blocking and maintain good drive and leverage off the snap. His footwork is so quick for a player of his size, and his balance and core strength stand out. He is effective in both gap- and zone- blocking schemes. His only true weaknesses come from overextending his arms and getting off balance to dictate contact, and a lack of density when absorbing bull rushes.
strengths: Hands are consistent in their pre-punch placement Extremely impressive athlete Great awareness to look for work and block the most pressing defender Has a finisher’s mentality in the run game
weaknesses: Kick slides don't have a big stretch to them, but he can manage at 6-foot-8 Can overextend and get a little off balance and out over his skis, at times Arm length is adequate due to his overall frame
bottom_line: The NFL draft is all about finding players with size, speed and strength who have the IQ to use those traits optimally. That's Joe Alt, and that should spell a top-10 selection as a future long-term tackle.

profile: Amegadjie looks like a future pro on film when standing next to FCS-level competition. And when the ball is snapped, he plays like it. His 6-foot-5, 325-pound frame can succeed at tackle in the NFL, although he also started at guard for one season at Yale. His feet are heavy at times, given his weight, but his strides cover a ton of ground to mirror defenders. His power at the point of attack is imposing. He brings consistent and impactful power to redirect and displace defenders. Though a bit high-waisted and high in his pad level, he shows a good understanding of winning with leverage, loading his body as low as he can before contact.
strengths: Body is built for the NFL Stride length on his kick slides and shuffles covers a lot of ground to stay in front of guys Really good balance of weight and power at contact Though he has a naturally high pad level, he is conscious of leverage and attempts to dip his shoulders before contact Very impressive displacement/redirect power versus his current competition
weaknesses: High pad level. High-waisted build at the hips makes it tough for him to sit in his stance at the snap Foot speed is somewhat slow Lack of hip flexibility and ability to sit in pass protection creates some balance issues
bottom_line: Projecting a player to go from the FCS level to the NFL level as a starter is tricky, but Amegadjie has the tools and the tape to be a worthwhile investment in the top 50 as a starting-caliber tackle or guard.

profile: Barton should switch from OT to the interior (likely center) in the NFL. He has good quickness and explosiveness from a loaded stance, where he can get low and load his weight on his quads before the snap. His grip strength is impressive, although his tendency to not let go leads to some holding calls. He has a mean streak in the run game with the leg drive to bury defenders. He is a good athlete off the ball and in space to be a successful second-level blocker. Barton struggles against power and will need to improve his anchor against interior defenders. He is experienced at tackle, but his foot speed and length are issues there.
strengths: Well-balanced in his pre-snap base. Butt is a bit high, but he is loaded on his quads to explode off the snap Strong grip strength Has a mean streak in the run game Boasts the athletic ability and coordination to get to the second level and be effective Excellent leg drive, especially on combo blocks Reliable hand placement to control defenders
weaknesses: Strength trails off after initial punch Grip strength is a plus, but his tendency to clamp on leads to holding penalties Gets tripped up/plays on the ground too much Can get on his toes too much and overextend Foot speed and length are not at the level of an NFL tackle
bottom_line: Barton is a tough lineman who moves well and has strong hands and a mean streak in the run game. His best position in the NFL is likely at center, as he brings starting-caliber traits there.

profile: Beebe brings experience and versatility from his Kansas State career, with 48 starts combined at left guard, left tackle and right tackle. He is built well for the interior, with a thick lower body, upper body and midsection. His trump card is his football IQ. He has an impressive understanding of why the fundamentals win at the position — leverage, hand placement, angles, timing, etc. Beebe leaves much to be desired as an athlete. He does not get off the ball with explosiveness and thus does not convert speed to power at the punch often. His feet are heavy, and he struggles to recover against twitchier pass rushers.
strengths: Brings a high football IQ and displays a great understanding of angles, leverage and timing Versatile lineman with experience at all three spots on the line Hands are well placed and effective Can effectively move defenders when he maintains good pad level/leverage Good size and technique to anchor straight bull rushes
weaknesses: Below-average athlete Lets defenders get across his face too easily and struggles to recover Feet are heavy to recover versus twitchier pass rushers Slow off the ball. Doesn't convert speed to power consistently
bottom_line: Beebe's high football IQ should lead to a long NFL career. Unfortunately, his athletic limitations will likely limit that career to that of a backup swing lineman.

profile: Bortolini's athletic potential has always been evident. He earned starts at left guard, right guard and center at Wisconsin but projects best to center in the NFL. He can explode out of his stance to reach and wall off defenders, and be effective as a puller on man/gap run-blocking plays. He is a high-intelligence lineman with good hand technique and makes protection calls at the line. His strength is adequate for single blocks, but he isn't a people-mover and may struggle with bigger NFL defensive linemen. Bortolini's biggest weakness is a lack of length, which shows when he is trying to maintain blocks.
strengths: Made protection calls at the line of scrimmage for Wisconsin’s offense. Explosive out of his stance to get across the face or wall off defenders. Athletic and coordinated enough to line up linebackers between the shoulders at the second level. Fast, balanced footwork to mirror in pass protection.
weaknesses: Late to react to stunt loopers. Strength is adequate to hold up against single blocks, but he isn’t a people-mover and may struggle against stronger guys. Lack of length shows when trying to maintain blocks. Has some bad reps where he lunges and misses while trying to make up for lack of length.
bottom_line: Bortolini brings an alluring combination of versatility, high football IQ and top-tier athleticism. He has starter qualities, but his lack of length could be a deal-breaker for NFL success.

profile: Cohen is a powerful player with a strong lower and upper body, which gives him an impactful punch at contact. He has a finisher's mentality and wants to bury defenders. However, this can sometimes be a negative, as he will be fixated on finishing a block instead of taking a more imminent threat to the quarterback. His base is narrow, which gives him loaded power at the snap but balance issues afterward. Lateral movement also gives him some trouble, as it takes him a bit to stop and start.
strengths: Compact and powerful stance. Can really pack a punch at contact. Finisher's mentality that will bury defenders if he has the chance. Well above-average length for a guard.
weaknesses: Lateral movements get him in trouble, including when blocking in space as a puller. Has a good length advantage physically but did seem susceptible to push-pull moves. Sometimes loses control when he attempts to pancake defenders. Weight can get over his toes and off balance. Narrow causes some imbalance after the snap.
bottom_line: Cohen gives you the power you're looking for as an NFL guard in a man/gap run scheme, but he does need to improve flexibility and anticipation to have better balance and become a more reliable pass protector to get and keep a starting role.

profile: Coleman has played both left tackle and guard for TCU. His wingspan is massive, and he has great movement skills to go with good length. His feet are quick, and his first step is explosive. He can also move well laterally but does need to anticipate better when passing off defenders. His hand placement and pad level are inconsistent. He also has good core and grip strength to maintain blocks after contact.
strengths: Wingspan and arm length are a big plus. Very good mover — well-built and good all-around athleticism (basketball background). Good core strength and grip strength to latch onto defenders. Good explosiveness and lateral quickness. Has experience at both guard and tackle.
weaknesses: Doesn't have imposing pop and leg drive at contact. Hand placement can be wide, causing defenders to achieve better positioning. Has the ability to be a quick lateral mover but just needs to anticipate better. Pad level is generally high.
bottom_line: Coleman is the ideal developmental offensive line prospect with high percentile athleticism and measurables that present a starting caliber ceiling in the NFL with improved fundamentals.

profile: Driskell, a former basketball player, is a massive human being on the left side of the line of scrimmage. He has imposing size and strength, and he is a true people mover when he makes contact. He has nice balance to recover from his basketball days. His hand placement is inconsistent and too often ineffective. They are too wide and do not allow him to get controlling leverage inside. His feet are a bit heavy, but his strides are so long that it doesn't affect him much. Better speed rushers will likely still give him trouble in the NFL. I also wish he would play with more pride through the whistle.
strengths: Massive frame. When he can fully extend his arms with leverage, defensive linemen go flying. His feet are a bit heavy, but he makes up for it with long strides. Due to sheer size, when he hits with momentum, he can displace defenders, especially on combination blocks. Has good balance for a big man.
weaknesses: Does not play with a fiery level of competitiveness. Hands are heavy and late too often. Hand placement is consistently wide right now. His pass protection is more about shoving defenders off their rush path than truly staying in front.
bottom_line: Driskell is a massive, powerful left tackle who would work well in a man/gap scheme, where his job is to vertically displace defenders. Even with his slow foot speed, if he can improve his hand placement, he can be a depth tackle prospect.

profile: If it's true that offensive linemen are the best athletes on the field, Fashanu is the poster child. His pass-blocking work is so impressive because of his fast feet. His power profile is adequate but not elite. In the run game, he does not pack a punch at contact and has some flexibility/footwork issues that don't allow him to maintain blocks. He uses a low-hands technique seemingly to make up for a lack of natural pad leverage, as well as to keep pass rushers from knocking his hands away. However, the low hands expose his chest too often. When he does get his arms up and in, he can anchor — even against good speed-to-power rushers.
strengths: Impressive athlete for a player of his size Great foot speed and balance Ability to anchor actually isn't as bad as advertised When he gets his hands inside, he rarely lets the opposition counter him
weaknesses: Hands were low in pass protection in 2022; exposes his chest and magnifies deficiencies versus power Some natural stiffness; high pad level, shorter strides in kick slides, narrow base to sustain run blocks Needs more of a mean streak in the run game
bottom_line: Fashanu is not only incredibly talented but will also be one of the youngest prospects in the 2024 class. He is the type of athlete in the trenches you draft in the first round, even if he needs to get stronger to live up to his very high potential.

profile: Fautanu is one of the best athletes in this offensive line class. His flexibility, agility and coordination could allow him to see meaningful reps at all five offensive line spots, but his long- term home is likely at guard or center. He has fast hands for flashes, repositioning and first contact. He also has a motor that never quits and looks to finish defenders whenever he can. Fautanu's aggressiveness is nice to see, but it can get him in trouble. He tends to overextend when punching and oversetting in pass protection. His power profile is good only when he has momentum. His lack of lower-half weight shows up when he is asked to anchor.
strengths: Flexible groin/hips to sit low and get his butt down in his pre-snap stance Fast feet that fire off the ball in run and pass blocking Impressive overall athlete for his size. Full OL position flexibility Has a leg drive that just doesn't quit Excellent hand work to flash/reset/latch on, etc.
weaknesses: Combo-block strength is hit-or-miss Has some reps where he gets overaggressive Lacks weight in the lower half Power is good when he has momentum. If not, it is not dominant
bottom_line: Fautanu is a true athlete of an offensive lineman with starting- caliber traits for center or guard. His movement skills would be a big plus in a zone-blocking scheme.

profile: Fisher is a two-year starter at right tackle for the Fighting Irish. He wins with power in run blocking and pass blocking. He has a wide, strong base that allows him to generate a ton of power through his lower half, making for an impactful punch at contact. He is an ideal comb/duo run blocker for a man/gap scheme. Fisher also checks the box for being able to displace and redirect pass rushers. His foot speed is somewhat limited, and because of that, he may always struggle with speed rushers who attack his outside shoulder. His size and power do mitigate that, though.
strengths: Wide base at the snap to get in a three-point stance for run blocking Impactful combo/duo blocker. Would fit well in a predominantly man/gap scheme Strong player at the point of attack who can really displace and redirect defenders
weaknesses: Feet hop more than move. Too much time with both feet not grounded Overextended too often Foot speed might be too slow to really protect the outside shoulder without a good jump
bottom_line: Fisher has the power to play at the pro level but needs to get quicker to his landmarks. He also needs to be more patient and balanced in his strikes to not be susceptible to NFL level speed rushers. He has starter potential at an ideal age.

profile: Foster has been a three-year starter for the Missouri Tigers, all at left tackle (over 900 snaps in each season). His experience is a plus, as he understands angles, leverage, hand usage, and just how to win at the position. While he is explosive for his size to get out of his stance, he is not a very flexible. He has a narrow base pre-snap and on the hoof, which causes some balance issues. He also plays with a high pad level, so despite showing a good understanding of leverage, he doesn't always maintain it. His zone-blocking grades are much higher than his gap scheme grade, as he's better with movement in space than brute strength.
strengths: Nice understanding of angles and leverage. Has decent strength to displace edge rushers. Not a flexible athlete but can be explosive out of his stance (evidenced by vertical and broad jump testing).
weaknesses: Base is a bit narrow, which causes his hips to be higher at the snap. Naturally high-waisted, which leads to a high pad level. Lacks flexibility in the lower half/groin to really stretch on his kick slides. Balance can be suspect, likely due to his narrow base. Will swing his arms back to generate power.
bottom_line: Foster has good length and experience to be a preferred backup offensive tackle in a zone-blocking scheme with enough dependability to be considered a potential starter.

profile: Frazier has the perfect background for an interior offensive lineman, as he was a four-time state wrestling champion in high school. That built-in core strength is a massive boon to his work on the interior. His body control and forearm/grip strength allow him to latch on to defenders. His flexibility is impressive, and he can get low to consistently win with leverage at the snap, even on quarterback sneaks. His arms are short, which is OK for a center, but he will lose cross-face reps against longer defensive linemen. He won't blow you up with power at contact, but he does have the weight, power and technique to anchor well in pass protection.
strengths: Fantastic flexibility Core strength and body control are a big plus High offensive line IQ Can get low enough for QB sneaks Adequate overall athleticism to shuffle and climb to the second level Excellent forearm/grip strength to latch on
weaknesses: A little too easy for defenders to toss aside, even when he has good hand placement Can get into trouble when longer interior defenders get across his face
bottom_line: Frazier's background and build give him a high floor as a scheme-versatile center who is worthy of an early Day 2 pick and a starting role.

profile: Fuaga is the kind of ass-kicker every NFL team wants in the trenches. He has a finisher’s mentality in the run game and takes pride in pushing defenders against their will. In pass protection, his stride length is limited but his foot speed makes up for it. He has a good, wide base to neutralize bull rushes quickly. His hands are consistently up and in the right position to strike with power at any moment. He also possesses the hand quickness to hand fight yet protect his chest. He can be a bit overzealous to make contact in pass protection, which can lead to a vulnerability to swipes and chops. But that patience did improve in 2023.
strengths: Fires off the ball with bad intentions (both in pass protection and run blocking) Good, wide base for quickly mitigating bull rushes Looks to bury defenders out of the play in run blocking Good grip strength to maintain blocks Very fast hands to punch yet recover and replace when getting into hand fights
weaknesses: Lighter in the lower body; holds a good amount of weight in his midsection Can get overzealous in making contact Can struggle reaching deeper landmarks in pass protection due to stride length (not foot speed)
bottom_line: Ultimately, Fuaga’s tape is that of a starting NFL offensive lineman, whether that is at tackle or guard. He brings the powerful mentality needed to stand out in the trenches. I believe he has the adequate length and foot speed, good offensive line IQ and elite strength to succeed at tackle and get a shot there as a first-round pick.

profile: Goncalves started at both right and left tackle for Pittsburgh over the past three seasons. While he isn't the best athlete, his foot speed is quick, which allows him to redirect and mirror better than one would expect. His hands are fast, and he remains calm when hand-fighting and resetting. He loves to use a hand flash move to bait defenders into throwing their hands first so he can counter or knock them away. He can move people in the run game and has good coordination for second-level blocks. When dealing with bull rushes, he is lighter in the lower half. His vulnerability to inside moves might cause him to play guard in the NFL.
strengths: Good knowledge of what wins at the position Fast, well-positioned hands. Will bait pass rushers with hand flashes Very competitive offensive lineman Feet are fast and controlled Great grip strength
weaknesses: Doesn't recover as easily as others when caught off guard Arm length may just be adequate at best for NFL thresholds Gives up the inside shoulder too easily Below-average athleticism
bottom_line: Goncalves’ 2023 season was cut short due to a season-ending torn ACL. He won't "wow" with athleticism or length, but he's a solid prospect who has the chance to be a starter at tackle or guard in the NFL.

profile: Guyton is a rare athlete for an offensive tackle. He is a former defensive end and didn't start playing offensive tackle until he got to college. That inexperience is still visible. His strike targets to defenders' bodies are inconsistent, as is his hand placement. This has caused him to be more of a pusher than a blocker. But his natural physical ability is evident. Guyton’s foot speed and stride length for a player of his size are impressive, allowing him to mirror without overextending. He can fire off the ball quickly, and that gives him a good punch at contact.
strengths: Truly elite movement skills. Could honestly play tight end Fires off the ball. Defensive end background shows up there Kick slides cover a ton of ground without him having to overextend and get off balance Good power with initial punch Evolved hand techniques from 2022 to 2023
weaknesses: Strike placement is off, allowing defenders to more easily roll off his blocks Hand placement is very inconsistent when it comes to strike locations and gripping the right spots to maintain blocks Late to react to stunts/twists/delayed rushes More of a pusher than a blocker High pad level at the snap
bottom_line: Guyton is raw in how to win with technique at the position, but there aren't many offensive linemen who have a better athletic mold. He has starting-caliber NFL gifts but must eliminate negatives in both the run and pass games to succeed at the next level.

profile: Haynes was a four-year starting right guard at UConn. He has the ideal build for an interior offensive lineman: shorter in height for leverage but higher in weight with long arms. His weight is also distributed well, especially in the lower half, which allows him to anchor bull rushes and throw down lighter defenders. He has a good first step off the line of scrimmage, and that makes for some impactful blocks as a puller and a zone blocker. His overall athleticism is good, but he can get off balance when in space. He isn't as much of a people-mover in a man- or gap-blocking scheme. He also doesn't sit as low as he should in pass protection.
strengths: Makes for a great puller and zone blocker Overall athleticism is above average. First step is better than top speed Consistent and strong hand placement to control/throw defenders Properly distributed weight. Good mass in the lower half Ideal build for an interior lineman. Short in height for leverage but above-average weight and arm length
weaknesses: Not nearly as effective when blocking up the middle in man/gap than as a puller or on zone-blocking plays Doesn't sit in pass protection like he needs to Balance can be an issue
bottom_line: Haynes showed in his tape and at the Senior Bowl that he has starting-potential measurables and traits at guard in the NFL. His best work comes on the move, which would bode well for a zone-blocking scheme and as a puller for man/gap schemes.

profile: Jones started his high school athletic career playing soccer and didn't start football until his junior season, where he played defensive end before offensive tackle. He played at Texas for six years and started 48 games. That experience is evident in his understanding of leverage, angles and hand placement. His long arms/wingspan can engulf on- and off- ball linebackers. He is a good linear athlete who can function in zone-blocking schemes. However, he will bend at the waist in pass protection with slower footwork, which will get him in trouble in the NFL. His power profile is adequate but not difference-making.
strengths: Strong, wide base in his stance allows him to fire off the ball with balance and power. Adequate athlete as a puller and for zone-blocking schemes. Long arms/wingspan to engulf linebackers at the second level. Fundamentally sound offensive tackle who has good hand placement and understanding of angles and leverage. Good grip strength to maintain blocks.
weaknesses: Seven holding penalties over the last two seasons. Lacks difference-making punch power. A little light in the pants to anchor and displace. Can get a little over his skis/toes when making contact, as bending at the waist will get him exposed against good edge rushers. Though a good athlete, his feet can be a bit heavy/slow.
bottom_line: Jones has a ton of experience, good length, and good linear athleticism for zone-blocking schemes. However, he still has some bad tendencies to clean up before he can be considered a rotational or starting tackle in the NFL.

profile: Keegan started 39 games at left guard for Michigan across four seasons. His height doesn't translate to length, as his arm length and wingspan are below the 25th percentile for the position. He is a natural athlete with good flexibility. He can sink low in his wide stance at the line of scrimmage for maximum leverage and explosion out of his stance. He has an impressive success rate when lining defenders up between the shoulders in space and at the second level. This leads to successful blocks in gap/man schemes. Keegan lacks the body density to quickly anchor, and although he can maintain blocks well, he is too easily moved by stronger defenders.
strengths: Coordinated athlete. Covers ground and stays balanced. Good flexibility in hips/groin to sink low in a wide base at snap. Good pad level despite height. Consistent hand placement and maintains blocks well. Impressive success rate when lining guys up in space and at the second level. Doesn’t panic and lunge at defenders. Good eyes for help in pass protection/passing off defenders.
weaknesses: Is manipulated too easily when locked up with stronger defenders. Lacks the body density for a quick anchor.
bottom_line: Keegan is smart and experienced, and he brings coordination, balance and explosiveness as an ideal guard in a man/gap scheme. He lacks true power and body density, which complicates his ceiling, but he does have starting-caliber traits.

profile: Latham is a dream offensive tackle physically, placing well above the 50th percentile at the position in height, weight and length. Yet, he moves like a player who is 40 pounds lighter. His foot speed and coordination are impressive. He has the flexibility to sit low in his stance at the line of scrimmage for good leverage. He is a true people mover in zone and gap concepts and is a devastating combo blocker. He shows good hand usage and hand speed for baiting pass rushers and resetting his hands after hand fighting. He sometimes struggles to anchor in pass protection, with his worst plays over the past two years coming against strong bull rushes.
strengths: Natural, athletic pre-snap stance Footwork is naturally very balanced and coordinated Shows an understanding of advanced techniques, such as baiting defenders by flashing his hands Arm length is more than adequate for the position at the pro level Hands are up, active and fast for initial contact and resetting Has the power to be a people mover
weaknesses: For his size, he isn't as imposing with strength as one would think Anchor ability is good due to size and wide base, but he does get punched back a bit on bull rushes Dips his head/eye level too often; allows defenders to counter/swim/avoid the block Can get overaggressive in his pass sets, which opens him up to inside moves
bottom_line: Latham is in the mold of an offensive lineman who does not come around often. He will be just 21 years old during his rookie season yet has two years of starting experience in the SEC. Despite garnering 18 penalties over the past two years and having room to improve in some anticipation parts of the position, Latham is a first-round trench player due to his rare combination of size, speed and refinement.

profile: Laumea played defensive tackle and offensive tackle in high school, and he'll bring positional versatility to the NFL, too. He won't be playing both sides of the ball, but he did gain experience at guard and tackle at Utah — though he projects best to guard. He has the size, thickness and power to handle NFL defensive tackles. He has a good punch at contact and can anchor well. His hand usage improved over the years but is still inconsistent when sustaining blocks. His foot speed appears to be an issue, and he struggles to mirror faster defenders. He has a good first step but lacks the long speed to climb to the second level.
strengths: Good power at contact. Adequate size to anchor and handle power. Good core strength to wall off defenders if he gets them between the shoulders. Has experience at right guard and right tackle.
weaknesses: First punch of contact is good, but he struggles to keep defenders blocked. Hands can be too wide and at the shoulders. Slow feet to react and mirror when defenders go cross-face. Decent first step, but he lacks the running speed to get to second-level defenders.
bottom_line: Laumea’s power profile is that of a potential starting guard. His footwork and anticipation must improve to match the speed of NFL rushers.

profile: Leveston was a two-year starter at left tackle at Kansas State, but his best NFL position is on the inside. That's not due to lack of length, as he has adequate weight and length for the guard position. His experience at tackle also gives him a more comfortable baseline for pass sets at guard. He is quite the mauler in the run game, and his frame allows him to generate a ton of power at contact. He is also a fighter when he gets latches onto defenders. His hands are his biggest weakness as a player right now. His hands are too low, which exposes his chest and makes him late to punch. His low hands also cause his hand placement to be too wide.
strengths: Thick, powerful build that can really move people. Lot of fight when he gets his hands locked on defenders. Pass set experience from tackle will be an advantage at guard. Feet are decently light for his size.
weaknesses: Low hands expose his chest too easily. Hands are too wide at contact too often.
bottom_line: Leveston has the build, strength and movement ability of a starting guard in the NFL, but his hand work must improve in order to achieve that.

profile: Limmer enters the NFL with a ton of experience, starting for the majority of the past four seasons. He has taken snaps at guard and center, but center is likely his best position in the NFL. He has good lower-half flexibility and explosiveness to get out of his stance and drive the legs when engaged with blockers. He also has quick and precise hand placement, which helps mitigate his lack of length. Although Limmer is strong, it feels like he could use more weight — both for anchoring and displacing stronger defenders. He is a coordinated athlete who can also be reliable on second-level blocks.
strengths: Looks to make contact until the whistle. Reliable hand quickness and placement to handle nose tackles. Has the first-step explosiveness to reach and get across a defender’s face at the snap. Coordinated and balanced leg drive when engaged in blocks.
weaknesses: Strength appears adequate. Could struggle with stronger NFL defensive linemen. Appears light when anchoring. Might need to add more weight.
bottom_line: Limmer is an experienced offensive lineman with consistent fundamentals, especially hand placement and leverage. He could use more weight to anchor better but should be a good depth player with starting potential.

profile: Mahogany is a throwback type of interior offensive lineman whom run-heavy teams will gravitate toward. He is built well for a guard, with a barrel chest, good weight in his midsection and plenty of sand in the pants (weight in the hamstrings and glutes). This helps him generate a ton of force in run blocking. He has an eraser's mentality and will completely block his guy out of the play. His pass protection needs polish, as his hands are often too low and he makes it easy to get across his face or swipe. His flexibility is also limited, which affects how well he can mirror. But he does bring strength to pass protection when his hands latch on.
strengths: Good build for an interior player. Big chest and midsection with good arm length Power at punch is very impressive Mentality is to bury defenders when he gets the chance Below-average athlete — but a coordinated one Comfortable and confident in man/gap combo-blocking systems
weaknesses: Despite longer arms, has a tough time getting into a two-point stance due to lack of flexibility Low hand can get him in trouble in pass protection. Makes it easier to swim/club-rip
bottom_line: Mahogany is a guard only and a powerful run blocker with inconsistencies in the passing game. He projects into a rotational and potential starting role for a team that is heavier in the run game in mostly man/gap concepts.

profile: McCormick will enter the NFL with 57 consecutive starts and three years of team captainship under his belt. He was a true mauler at South Dakota State. He will fight defenders in a phone booth and has a leg drive that goes through the whistle, though not overly so.
