He is a 98th-percentile athlete for the position in the broad and vertical jumps, and you can see that in how he gets out of his stance. He has a narrow base, likely due to some stiffness in his hips/groin. This causes him to struggle with adjusting once moving. It also forces his pad level to be higher at the snap, as he cannot sink his butt as low in his stance.
strengths: Imposing player who dominated his level of competition at South Dakota State. Has a finisher's mentality. Keeps legs driving through the whistle. Willing to "fight in a phone booth" in between the tackles. Explosive out of his stance with good foot speed for zone and pulling responsibilities.
weaknesses: A bit stiff in his change of direction and flexibility movements. Base is more narrow, which causes him to be higher at the snap. Naturally narrow stance causes some additional imbalance.
bottom_line: McCormick brings a mauling mentality with explosive athleticism to the guard position. He's a tad stiff in the hips, which limits his flexibility, but he has starting potential in a zone-blocking scheme.

profile: McMahon has started at right guard, left guard and center, though center is likely his best chance of finding a starting NFL role. He has a compact frame, which gives him good body control and precise short-area explosiveness. He can really fire off the ball and is often the first to dictate contact with fast, inside hands. He lacks the length to really hold onto blocks against typical NFL-sized rushers. He also struggles to really anchor against players with above-average power.
strengths: Smaller build gives him compact short-area movements and body control. Feet are light and quick. Can get hand defenders very quickly — almost always the first to initiate contact. Hand placement is well-timed and placed. Lots of interior offensive line versatility.
weaknesses: Even for a center, length is an issue — below 10th percentile arm length and wingspan. Lacks the strength to really maintain blocks. Doesn't have the density to anchor for long.
bottom_line: McMahon is a versatile interior offensive lineman who wins with quickness and consistent fundamentals. However, he likely lacks the length and strength of a starting-caliber offensive lineman in the NFL.

profile: It's hard to believe how the 6-foot-7, 340-pound Mims can sit down in his stance and run to cover ground. He also has elite length for the position. While his physical potential is through the roof, he lacks experience. He played only 682 snaps over the past two seasons with just eight starts, due to biding his time at a talented program and injury in 2023. He is a strong player who can maintain blocks well with good upper-body strength. Mims is more smooth than he is truly explosive as an athlete, which takes away some of his punch at contact. His feet are also a bit slow in pass protection, which can cause some clunky kick backs and oversetting.
strengths: Ideal build and elite length for the pro level Fast and fluid movement skills for a player of his size; moves like a giant athlete Impressive flexibility to sit in his stance pre-snap and get a wide base Strong player who can displace and redirect Grip strength is strong when he gets his hands inside
weaknesses: Feet are heavy Kick slides are a bit slow and strides don't stretch as far as they could, appearing a little clunky in the lower body He is a smooth athlete, especially for his size, but doesn't fire off the ball like Broderick Jones did Inexperienced. Doesn't seem as confident in pass sets
bottom_line: Mims is not a polished prospect — a level below former teammate and first-round pick Broderick Jones — but he brings sky-high potential. He'll take some developing, but trench players built like this don't make it out of the top 50.

profile: Morgan is a smooth-moving prospect whose best position in the NFL might be guard. His track and field background gives him natural balance and core strength for good change-of- direction ability. His arm length isn't elite for offensive tackle play, but it should be adequate. While his footwork is fast, the strides in his kick slide are short. His hand placement, patience and football IQ are all pluses. Though listed at 325 pounds, he lacks density and strength. Bull rushes can overwhelm him if they come at an angle, and though he has the foot speed to stay in front of pass rushers, he doesn't have the natural strength to redirect their momentum.
strengths: Nice overall athlete with good explosiveness and good running speed Wide, imposing base in his stance Strong hand placement in pass protection Good core strength for change of direction and quick reaction to stunts/games
weaknesses: Can get pushed around a bit, even when he's in front of defenders Has the athleticism to mirror pass rushers but doesn't always have the strength to redirect them Good anchor technique but lacks sand in the pants to truly stop them cold Shorter stride length on his kick slides
bottom_line: Morgan needs to get stronger, whether he's at tackle or guard in the NFL, but he has desirable athletic traits with fast hands and feet that bolster his starting-caliber potential.

profile: Nourzard is a versatile center prospect who shows the movement skills and football intelligence to play in a variety of NFL offenses. His base is both wide and loaded, which allows him to play with good pad level while also allowing him to fire off the ball quickly. His wide base also allows him to anchor well. His hand placement is consistently inside and effective in locking defenders up. He doesn't really pack a punch at contact, even on combination blocks, and when it comes to stunts, he has a tough time adjusting to/anticipating the speed of looping defenders.
strengths: Wide yet loaded stance that allows him to fire off the ball and get across defensive tackles' face. Conscious of leverage and can keep a low pad level when moving. Feels so in control at all times. Understands the geometry of offensive line play — how to shift weight and wall players off. Hand placement is consistent and effective. Base is wide and balanced to anchor.
weaknesses: Doesn't really pack a punch at contact. Ohio State's athletes really gave him trouble. Late to see/adjust to loopers on stunts.
bottom_line: Nourzard presents a well-rounded skillset and high-floor fundamentals for almost any offense, though he must get stronger to really garner a full-time starting role in the NFL.

profile: Nugent spent most of his college career at Stanford before transferring to Michigan for the 2023 season. He is small for the position, at under 6-foot-2 and less than 300 pounds. However, he does have 62nd-percentile arm length for a center. His physical limitations show up often on his tape. Despite a decent first step, he does not cover much ground when running due to shorter strides. He is also without the strength or density to be a reliable anchor at the NFL level at his current weight. Nugent struggles to move laterally and can get exposed against quicker defensive linemen.
strengths: Arm length is above the 50th percentile for centers. His lack of height helps with leverage. Understands what to look at and where to be for angles and walling off defenders.
weaknesses: Consistently lacks the lateral quickness to recover against quicker interior offensive linemen. Appears to lack the strength to truly displace defenders. Gets pushed back too easily against bull rushers. Does not cover a lot of ground when on the move due to shorter strides.
bottom_line: Nugent brings good experience to the table but lacks the physical ability and build to be a starter or rotational lineman at the NFL level.

profile: The 6-foot-7 Paul started 44 games at Houston. In 2022, he won just by being big, but his pad level was high, his balance wasn't stable, his footwork was sloppy and his shoulders and upper back were hunched over and prone to overextension. In 2023, he improved his pre- and post-snap posture for better balance, leverage and strength. It wasn’t perfect, but it was encouraging. His arm length and wingspan are elite for the position. His foot speed and hand speed are slow, which allows defenders to get across his face and leads to inconsistent hand placement. He has the size and density to move people in the run game but lacks a true mean streak.
strengths: Good anchor ability Vines for arms Posture was much improved in 2023 Footwork and initial kick slides were clunky in 2022, but first-step coordination/explosiveness improved in 2023
weaknesses: Feet are a bit heavy, which is not unexpected due to his size Arms/hand placement is still erratic, at times. Strike zone is not consistent and inside enough Hand speed is somewhat slow Lacks intensity as a run blocker
bottom_line: Paul's size alone makes him worth betting on, and his improvement in his fundamentals from 2022 to 2023 was encouraging. He has the frame of a starting-caliber offensive tackle but does need to get quicker and more fundamentally sound — particularly with his hands and feet — to become a reliable long-term lineman.

profile: There just aren't many holes in Powers-Johnson's game, especially since he moved to center. He has complete positional versatility along the interior offensive line. He has a fire hydrant-like build with short arms and a barrel chest/belly, but that build makes him powerful. He has the upper-body strength to bench-press 300-pound defensive linemen and the density to anchor quickly and effectively. He is light on his feet for his size, can climb to the second level and has good balance from his wrestling days.
strengths: A big-time people-mover in the run game Big chest and midsection help generate a ton of upper-body strength Dense player who can anchor quickly and effectively Destroyer-of-worlds type of mentality Very good grip strength to toss defenders to the side
weaknesses: Short arms, even for an interior player
bottom_line: Powers-Johnson possesses starting-caliber power and finesse traits at center or guard for both zone or man/gap-blocking concepts. He is dominant enough at his position to be considered a top-20 talent.

profile: Puni was a no-star recruit and played at Central Missouri for four seasons before transferring to Kansas in 2022, where he played left guard and left tackle. In his first season with the Jayhawks (left guard), Puni displayed bad posture and poor pad level. That made him susceptible to rushers and didn't allow him to really maintain blocks. His posture was better in 2023 (left tackle), and although he was still standing taller than preferred, he was conscious of leverage and dropped his pads more before contact. He also showed a lot more power in 2023, disrupting and displacing defenders. His power best projects to guard.
strengths: Massive player who is tough to get around from size alone Has the power to displace people when he gets them between the shoulders
weaknesses: Poor pad level in 2022 but improved in 2023. Might be a hindrance at guard Upright stance after the snap exposes his chest and makes him too easy to manipulate Top heavy in his weight but played with a flatter back in 2023 Does not maintain blocks on tape
bottom_line: Puni is much improved from 2022 to 2023, and if he continues on his current trajectory, he has the power profile and size to earn a rotational role at guard with starting potential.

profile: Robinson is a well-built guard who has a ton of athletic potential. However, his inconsistencies need work if he is to even be considered a preferred backup. His well-distributed weight gives him good leg drive for run blocking and double teams. He also has good burst out of his stance to get on the move as a puller. His upper body doesn't have the power that his lower body does. That, plus a lack of consistent pad level, makes it too easy for defenders to throw him off. Robinson also gets off double teams too quickly and can miss his aiming points when lining up defenders in space. His arm length is a plus, but his hand placement is too wide.
strengths: Well-built offensive lineman whose lower half is good for leg drive. Stretched, wide base at the snap makes it tough to get into a gap next to him. Good first-step burst out of his stance. Quick, balanced footwork from a wide base makes him tough to get around.
weaknesses: Comes off double teams too quickly Upper-body strength can be an issue, at times, as defenders can throw him off to get off blocks. Misses his aiming points when asked to block at the second level. Hands are often too wide and expose his chest. Lacks consistency in pass protection.
bottom_line: Robinson is a good project interior lineman for a zone-blocking scheme. He needs to work on his pass-blocking consistency to become a preferred depth player or a starter.

profile: Rosengarten's most alluring trait is how he moves. He is light and explosive on his feet, as evidenced by his 90th-percentile 40-yard dash time. He can really get out of his stance and into defenders quickly, even at the second level. He does struggle with power. Even with momentum, he struggles to displace defenders. When asked to go one-on-one with more powerful defensive ends, he wouldn't give up the fight, but he would give up ground. He does play with a chip on his shoulder and a mean streak to his game, which isn't something you see often from more finesse linemen.
strengths: Lighter weight, but he can really move. Nimble despite being an OT. High-motor player. Looks like he plays with a chip on his shoulder. Has a mean streak, even without a lot of natural power.
weaknesses: Struggles to generate difference-making power at the point of attack. Got into trouble when asked to block bigger players. Does not sustain blocks consistently.
bottom_line: Rosengarten is worth a Day-3 flier as a developmental, athletic offensive tackle. He lacks the power necessary to survive at the NFL level in his current state.

profile: Rouse has played in and started a ton of games in his college career. He is a well-built and smart offensive lineman (biomechanical engineer at Stanford). He has a good understanding of hand placement and angles, and his eyes are consistently looking in the right place for the most dangerous rusher. As for traits, his power is adequate for the NFL. He can move well for his size, but his feet are slow to mirror rushers when he doesn't anticipate. He also has a bad tendency to dip his head at contact. His leverage is inconsistent (often playing high).
strengths: Well-built offensive lineman. Well above average arm length/wingspan. Good eyes on where to look when locking assignment is less obvious. Good understanding of hand placement. Power is adquate for the NFL.
weaknesses: Slow to react and mirror when he isn't able to anticipate. Does not play with consistent leverage; makes contact high. Head/eyes dip too often at contact.
bottom_line: Rouse is an experienced and well-built offensive tackle prospect with good size, length and football intelligence for a man/gap run scheme. In pass protection, he must improve his foot speed and consistency with leverage in order to become a starter at the next level.

profile: Suamataia is an impressive overall athlete with difference making explosiveness and power in the run game. Whether blocking in man/gap or zone concepts, he has the upper and lower body strength to drive and displace. In pass pro, his footwork is natural for a player of his size, but he doesn't move laterally as well as he does forward. Where he is a dream athlete for a tackle, his inexperience leaves his technique in a raw and inconstistent state. His hand placement and timing are a work in progress, and at times he can be more of a shover than a true blocker.
strengths: Versatile starting experience Has impressive posture, weight distribution and balance for a player of his size Upper and lower body power to drive and displace Really explosive athlete in the run game
weaknesses: Hand placement/timing is too inconsistent and ineffective He is more of a shover than a blocker right now Is green on pass blocking experience; reacting instead of anticipating He can play too upright and abandons pad level in pass pro Explosive off the ball in run blocking, but a bit off balance and not quite the same athlete in pass pro/laterally
bottom_line: Suamataia is a dream prospect to draft and develop somewhere on day two. I worry about him being baptized by fire if drafted in the first round and called upon to start right away.

profile: Thomas didn't play offensive line until he got to ULL, so it is well within reason to believe his best football is still ahead of him. He is a powerful offensive tackle who has a finisher's mentality in the run game. He can anchor well versus speed- to-power in pass protection, and he has good core strength to maintain blocks. His feet are heavy, both in pass protection and when run blocking. His hand placement seems to always be targeted inside, and he does have good power at punch.
strengths: Powerful offensive tackle who has a man/gap blocking mentality. Good core strength to stay balanced through twists and turns. Finisher's mentality who wants to bury his defenders or walk them to the sideline. Can anchor well against speed-to-power moves.
weaknesses: Not very fleet of foot — teams won't want him zone-blocking too often. Heavy, slow feet in pass protection leave his inside shoulder susceptible. Kickslide footwork is not very balanced.
bottom_line: If you keep things in a phone booth, Thomas has the power profile to make the roster as a depth offensive tackle in a man/gap scheme offense.

profile: Van Pran is a smart center prospect who projects well to a man/gap scheme in the NFL. He started at center for three straight seasons, and with that workload comes an understanding of how to win with hand placement, leverage and footwork, in addition to pre-snap communication. His strength is adequate, and his hand placement allows him to latch consistently. His wide base gives him a good ability to anchor, but it hinders how well he can mirror in pass protection. His weaknesses show up when he is required to be agile in one-on-ones. More athletic pass rushers gave him trouble. He sets the tone with physical play on every snap.
strengths: Wider base in pass protection makes him powerful to anchor Overall athleticism is below average, but burst/first step quickness is good High football IQ Good hand placement/hand strength Does not shy away from the physicality of the position. Great mentality
weaknesses: Wide base makes it easier to anchor but tougher to shuffle and mirror against stunt rushers Good in pass protection in a phone booth, but anything that makes him really move is a challenge
bottom_line: Van Pran is a high-IQ center prospect whose acumen, experience and physical mentality warrant a shot at a starting role (center only) in a man/gap-heavy scheme despite some athletic limitations.

profile: Zinter is a powerful interior offensive lineman whose skill set and size fit perfectly with Michigan's power running scheme. He carries a lot of weight in his upper half, giving him good power to push people at contact and latch on to maintain blocks. Despite his lack of weight in the lower half, he anchors well. He is a below-average athlete in movement and flexibility. His size is his best attribute in pass protection, but he is also patient as a pass blocker.
strengths: Good combo block play in power run-blocking concepts Leg drive doesn't quit once he latches on Powerful player who can displace when he hits Upper-body power to anchor despite being lighter in the lower half Size is his best attribute in pass protection. Also shows good patience
weaknesses: Nimble footwork for a player of his size Light in the pants. Most of his weight and power comes from above his waist Stiff at the hip. A little hunched over in his posture Below-average athlete for the guard position Taller height gives him more length but also makes it tougher for him to get low for leverage, especially with hip stiffness
bottom_line: Zinter's movement limitations will likely limit him to man/gap schemes if he is to be successful at the next level, but he does have sufficient power to get a shot at a starting role at some point in such systems.

profile: Boyd's game is built around his power. His weight is appropriate for nose tackle responsibilities, which he executes very well at the FCS level. He is a build-up speed and power player. As a run defender, he is quite stout in a variety of alignments. His biggest detractor is his arm length, as it falls below thw 10th percentile length, which makes it tough for him to get off blocks and pull off pass rush moves. However, he could still stand to throw a good club move in there with as much power as he has, so there is still some upside.
strengths: Powerful leg drive that can really push the pocket, especially with speed-to-power momentum. Powerful crasher on stunts. Strong run defenders who held up well against double teams in the FCS.
weaknesses: Short arm length makes getting off blocks more of a chore. Build up speed more than twitched-up athleticism. Hands could get faster — could use more rush moves, even just club variations.
bottom_line: Boyd likely lacks the length to be a consistent difference-maker in the passing game, but his power and size make him a good candidate to be a backup defensive lineman in odd or even fronts.

profile: Carter, a three-time captain at Duke, brings a pass-rush profile that starts with a strong upper body and an ability to bench-press interior offensive linemen off-balance in his bull rushes. From there, you'll see him use club-rip, club-arm over and spin moves to diversify his pass-rush profile. As a run defender, he is reliable and can even hold up against double teams with good leverage. His overall athleticism feels average, mainly in pursuit speed, but he does have a quick first step. He is also an intelligent player who consistently knows where the ball is and where it is going.
strengths: Strong upper body. High football intellgience. Deep pass-rush bag of moves and counters. Good versatility. Strong player who can hold up against double teams when he gets leverage.
weaknesses: Get-off was below average in 2022 but improved in 2023. Pursuit speed is average for the NFL level.
bottom_line: Carter isn't an elite physical presence, but he is a versatile, smart and consistent football player in both the run and pass games. He projects as a high-floor rotational player with starting potential.

profile: He is a steady, impactful, fundamental and high-motor player on the interior who can play anything from a 4i to a 0-tech. His hand placement is consistent and effective, which allows him to make up for less-than-ideal measurables. He also sees gaps/blocking schemes before the snap and knows how to attack. The reason he isn't mocked higher is his physical limitations. Both his arm length and wingspan are below the 10th percentile, which limits a lot of his pass-rush potential. It also makes it tough to get off blocks against the run. He is also lighter in weight for a nose tackle, but his frame appears to be maxed out.
strengths: Intelligent football player who anticipates where the ball is going and how to attack blocking schemes right at the snap. Good initial burst out of his stance (72nd percentile 10-yard split). High motor player who does a lot of the dirty work on the interior. Consistent and effective hand placement. Can play anything from a 4i-0 tech (though you don't want him as a 3-4 DE).
weaknesses: Fire hydrant build, which comes with leverage benefits but also length deficiencies (arms and wingspan below 10th percentile). Any sort of turn and chase is tough for him due to his shorter strides. It is difficult for him to fully get off blocks due to his lack of length.
bottom_line: Davis has the football intelligence and mentality of a depth/rotational defensive lineman for any front. He has physical limitations, which hinder his pass-rush efficacy and block shedding, but he could still become a spot starter at some point due to his intangibles.

profile: Fiske played five seasons at Western Michigan, including three as a full-time starter, before transferring to Florida State in 2023. While the Power Five level presented a new challenge, he grew more comfortable over time. Fiske wins with a quick first step and fast hands, allowing him to be an effective one-gap penetrator and making him tough to reach block. His shorter arms limit the depth of his pass-rush tool bag despite his good understanding of moves. His club-arm over/swim is potent. His weight limits his strength in run defense, but he holds up well pound-for-pound and possesses good eyes and anticipation for where the ball is going.
strengths: Good ankle flexibility/ability to corner Active and fast hands Light but smart run defender High-motor player Quickness makes it so difficult to reach block
weaknesses: Lighter weight means he can get pushed around Shorter arms will show up as an issue
bottom_line: Fiske's measurements are not ideal, but he has an NFL-level football IQ and pass-rush quickness to be a potential impact player as a 4-3 defensive tackle, even with some run-defense deficiencies.

profile: Hall's best plays are eye-popping, but they are inconsistent. He gives up his chest/leverage and can be manipulated by smaller interior players too often. He also tends to try to shed a block instead of holding the line. He has an explosive first step for a player of his size, and his length on the interior can be devastating. Conditioning is a question because there are some reps where you can tell he's fresh and will shed a block/impose his will while he will abandon his technique and fundamentals to give up a chunk plays on other snaps.
strengths: Length is a big advantage for him versus shorter-armed interior defenders. Above average first-step explosiveness, especially for his size. Will get his long arms up and into throwing lanes. Hands can be violent and devastating.
weaknesses: Loses leverage too often, especially when asked to two-gap. Loses short-area control once he gets on the hoof — tough to stop his momentum. Inconsistent effort/explosiveness — conditioning could have been an issue in 2023. Prioritizes gap shooting/block shedding over gap integrity, at times.
bottom_line: Hall is a very alluring player because of what he brings to the defensive line from a physical and athletic standpoint. He has good rotational potential, but he must become more consistent in his anchor and run-defense responsibilities.

profile: At 6-foot-2, Hall is not long enough to be a 3-4/4-3 defensive end. And at 280 pounds, he's not big enough to be a full-time defensive tackle. However, his play is quite productive. At his lower weight, speed and quickness are his calling cards. He loves to get across an offensive lineman's face to shoot a gap and get into the backfield. He does this either with a fast club-arm over or by setting his blockers up with a Euro step before making a move. As a run defender, he is strong for his size, especially when he maintains a lower leverage. But inconsistent — too wide or too low — hand placement negates that, at times.
strengths: Can shoot gaps and get across the face of linemen with consistency. Looks like a basketball player with his euro-step set ups. Decent ability to corner.
weaknesses: Leg drive is lacking power and displacement strength, even against single blocks. Does not hold up well against combination blocks.
bottom_line: Hall's measurements make him a tough player to slot into a specific scheme, but due to how quickly he can win with finesse on the interior, his best spot in the league is likely as a DT/DE in a versatile 4-3 front. His pass-rush abilities give him the chance to be a productive pass-rush specialist.

profile: Harris is a compact interior defensive lineman who comes in at a lower weight. He has an explosive first step, fast hands, a good ability to shoot gaps and consistently wins the leverage and pad level battle. He'll be a liability in run defense outside of shooting gaps, and his significantly shorter arms make it tougher to get off blocks when the initial move doesn't hit.
strengths: Compact build gives him good explosiveness out of his stance. Good, natural leverage out of his stance. Strong enough to push-pull and disengage when he gets his hands inside. Quick arm over to disengage and meet backs at the line of scrimmage.
weaknesses: Shorter arms lead to missed tackles. Tougher for him to break free from offensive linemen that win the length battle.
bottom_line: Harris is a one-gap penetrating three-technique defensive tackle for a 4-3 defense whose measurables and run-defense limitations likely limit him to a rotational role as a pass-rusher.

profile: Jackson's game is all about quick penetration, which stems from a fast first step and arm-over move. His pass-rush profile is more limited, as he "plays the hits" more than wins with a diverse bag of moves; it’s not the worst thing, but it’s worth noting. His bull rush and push-pull can be effective if executed quickly, but his leg drive and displacement run out when offensive linemen get to their balance and anchor. He can get off blocks quickly in run defense, though he is inconsistent, likely due to his arm length, which ranks below the 50th percentile for defensive tackles. While he can hold up against double teams, it's not a given.
strengths: Quick one-gap penetrating defensive tackle Effective arm-over move The slipperiest 330-pounder you'll see
weaknesses: Gets moved easily by double teams Plays on the ground too much Bull rush has a nice push due to quickness, but does not sustain displacement Not an effective stunt player
bottom_line: Jackson is a slippery one-gap penetrating defensive lineman who can play nose and three-technique in a 4-3 scheme. A lack of arm length limits his pass-rush/starter potential, but he can be successful as a depth pass rusher in a rotation.

profile: Jefferson's biggest strength is his strength. He started weightlifting at a young age and even competed in high school. That power shows up in how he dictates contact, enabling him to stack and shed with control and violence. He can be slow to do so, however, which yields limited backfield production. His arms are average for interior defenders, but they seem smaller due to how he struggles to get his arm over on rush moves. He has a good first step to accelerate, but his shorter strides don't cover a ton of ground. He holds up well against double teams, something he will need to continue to do as a projected nose tackle.
strengths: Average arm length for defensive tackles in the NFL. Very strong player who did 34 repetitions on the bench press (weightlifting background). Really impressive core strength and body control. Good strength to stack and shed. Nice first step burst.
weaknesses: Good first step burst, but his shorter stride doesn't cover a ton of ground. Slower to disengage, which is why he did not have much backfield production.
bottom_line: Jefferson has the power of an NFL defensive lineman. He needs to speed up how quickly he gets into the backfield in order to really gain a rotational role in the pros.

profile: Jenkins is one of the strongest players in the draft. He is a run stopper at heart who is most comfortable and confident holding the line. His run-stop percentage ranks in the 99th percentile due to how well he can hold up against double teams and control one-on-one run-blocking situations. He has an explosive lateral first step that allows him to get across a guard's face and into gaps, but he does not bring that same level of explosiveness to getting upfield as a pass rusher. His biggest knock is arm length, which will likely be well below average for NFL standards. This appears as an issue when gaining leverage and separation through contact.
strengths: Holds up very well against double teams. Pound-for-pound, he might be the strongest player in the class. Effective at using the corkscrew technique. Really quick lateral first step to cross face/gaps.
weaknesses: Shorter arms will get exposed versus longer linemen. Short arms also prove to be an issue when trying to get distance/leverage when disengaging off blocks. Short arms also show up as a weakness when tackling. First step upfield in pass rush is not as explosive as his lateral step.
bottom_line: Jenkins is one of the strongest players in the entire draft class, but his arm-length limitations and lack of pass-rush profile will likely limit his draft stock to a mid-to-late Day 2 selection. However, his high floor presents starting potential in a 4-3 scheme.

profile: Lee is light (below the fifth percentile among DTs). That lack of weight obviously shows up and clouds his home position in the NFL, but if he can gain more weight and play between 285-290 pounds, he can be a solid player. He has fantastic quickness and agility for an interior defender. His shorter arms make block shedding tougher, but he has a nice rip move to attack shoulders. Despite his lack of weight, he is strong and gives great effort at all times.
strengths: Consistent inside hand placement. As expected with lighter weight, elite agility testing drills showcase good ability to corner and bend for an interior player. Quick first step and lateral agility to get across the face of interior offensive linemen. Has the speed to catch hesitant RBs from the backside. Understands corkscrew technique against doubles and executes it well.
weaknesses: Lighter weight does show up even though he has impressive strength. Run defense is more about gap shooting than holding the line (but he is better at the latter than you expect).
bottom_line: Lee has a unique build and skillset for an interior player, and his long-term future might be as an edge defender, but if you get get a bit more weight on him, he has the quickness and effort to be a potential rotational contributor in an even front as a three- technique defensive tackle.

profile: Lovett's height, weight and length are all big pluses physically on the inside. He's strong as an ox, and though he doesn't have many pass-rush moves, his push-pull and arm- over moves can be devastatingly violent. He can hold the point of attack very well against double teams to be a reliable nose tackle. Ultimately, his lower draft profile stems from a lack of first-step explosiveness and pass-rush plan.
strengths: Strong to take double teams in the middle. Violent push-pull and arm-over moves. Massive wingspan and arm length for an interior defender. Junkyard dog in the middle.
weaknesses: Slower off the ball and into offensive linemen — doesn't have impressive explosion off the snap. Doesn't really show much in terms of pass-rush moves (just looks to win with strength).
bottom_line: Lovett is a stout run defender with plus measurables to play in between the B-gaps in the NFL. His lack of pass-rush ability will likely limit him to a rotational player at best, but he can be a useful one for a run-defense role.

profile: The 6-foot-1, 305-pounder brings elite-level strength and athletic ability to trench play, earning a spot on Bruce Feldman's 2023 “Freaks List." Murphy's punch and press are violent and strong, allowing him to utilize his lower leverage to dictate run-defense battles. Teams may think they can run at him due to his measurables, but he has great lower-body strength and doesn't yield much ground versus combo blocks. Perhaps nothing better sums up Murphy’s strength than that he played nose tackle despite 360-pound T’Vondre Sweat's presence along Texas’ defensive line. His strength and explosiveness led to excellent pass-rush grades and win rates.
strengths: Strong player Violent. Throws offensive linemen aside in run defense Upper-body strength to bench press o-linemen with good leverage Punch and press are so imposing Explosive first step Great balance
weaknesses: Short arms can become an issue Doesn't have a deep set of pass-rush moves Needs to be quicker to go to counters/fight off blocks
bottom_line: Murphy is a gifted defensive lineman in both the strength and speed categories. He is a versatile three-down player who brings plus abilities as a run defender and a pass rusher, projecting as a first-round impact starter for any front.

profile: Newton, the 2023 Big Ten Defensive Player of the Year, is listed at only 6-foot-1.5 and 300 pounds, but he often makes up for it in quickness. Few pass rushers get off blocks better than him. He likes to win by getting his hands on a blocker and using a push-pull or arm over. He brings a wide variety of pass-rush moves and counters. In run defense, he shoots his hands up and in and throws linemen aside after getting them off-balance. If he does not immediately win, he can get controlled at his lower weight. His high run-defense grades come more from gap shooting than from holding the line, and he does not hold up consistently against double teams.
strengths: Possesses quick handwork Feet never stop firing Experienced and effective stunt/loop rusher Motor that never stops Explosive first step
weaknesses: You can tell he is light Lacks overall flexibility for getting low or bending on a rush High run-defense grade comes more from gap shooting and disengaging blocks than truly holding the line Top speed is limited in pursuit
bottom_line: Newton has some physical limitations due to his size and lack of natural flexibility, but his hand usage, pass-rush tools and block-shedding ability allow him to be very productive in any alignment as a three-to-five-technique player.

profile: Orhorhoro weighed just 265 pounds as an edge defender when he joined the Tigers but has since bulked up to around 290 to play inside, as well. His body type makes him a tweener on the defensive line, but he is strong for his frame, and that gives him a ton of versatility. He has played everything from zero-technique to five-technique. He is a reliable player in run defense, consistently staying square with the ball carrier at the line of scrimmage, and is not one to whiff on tackles. As a pass rusher, he wins with speed and power, but his profile outside of his athleticism is lacking — something that could develop during his NFL career.
strengths: Strong pound-for-pound player Versatile. Can line up anywhere from 0-tech to 5-tech Decent upper-body strength to bench press linemen and also push with a good bull rush Fundamentally sound run defender who keeps his shoulders square to the ball Good stunt player as a crasher or a looper
weaknesses: Leans too much on his athleticism to win as a pass rusher Sometimes struggles to disengage with proper speed due to shorter arms Change of direction and pursuit of athleticism are average
bottom_line: Orhorhoro is a versatile defensive lineman who can be a high- floor player at defensive end or defensive tackle. However, he needs to develop technical pass-rush moves to be more than a rotational player at the next level.

profile: Randolph is a high-effort player who wants to get into the backfield on every play. Illinois teaches their defensive linemen to stay square to the line of scrimmage in most situations, and Randolph can do that. His shuffle is adequate, but when asked to turn a corner, he struggles. He wants to get into the backfield every snap, which he does most effectively with an arm-over move. Outside of that, he doesn't have many pass-rush moves, though we have seen a good long arm and some chop-rip reps when aligned as a DE. His feet are heavy, at times, and that goes along with some overall ceiling of athleticism concerns.
strengths: High motor player. Decent first step. Violent hands for club and rip moves.
weaknesses: Can move side-to-side in a shuffle at the line of scrimmage, but there is tightness in his turns. Give up leverage pretty quickly. He tries the arm-over move instead of holding the line with a push-pull. Lacks overall athleticism to be a difference-maker as a pass -rusher. Feet look heavy at times.
bottom_line: Randolph projects as a depth player for even front who can align as 3-4 tech. His gap-shooting mentality will give him some splash plays, but he is inconsistent right now beyond that.

profile: Smith was a rotational starter as a true freshman at LSU, had his 2022 season ended by a torn ACL and then played 582 snaps in 2023. The 6-foot-6 interior defender’s size jumps out. He has the length and strength to play any alignment. His lack of snaps in college means he is green in the technical aspects of the game. His hands, while active, are often reckless. He leans more on athleticism than the fundamentals and can be a bit slow to react. His explosiveness is good when adjusting for weight, but his burst is lacking. He can hold up decently well in run defense against double teams but is slow to get off single blocks.
strengths: Unique build for a defensive tackle Long arms provide a lot of control to shoot his hand up and peek into the backfield versus the run Has the size and strength to hold ground against double teams Hand placement needs work, but when it's on point, he can dominate a rep
weaknesses: Slower off the ball Active but reckless hands Leg drive stalls out on bull rushes. Might not trust his knee Slow to see the ball and to disengage
bottom_line: Smith is a physically gifted prospect, but one who will need to develop. He has to speed up his play, both in recognition and movements, to be more than a rotational player with plus size.

profile: It has been a long journey — five years and 62 games played — for Sweat to become an NFL-caliber defensive tackle. In 2022, though he had the size to be an impact player, his hand usage, conditioning and lack of leverage limited his effectiveness. In 2023, he improved in all areas, as he no longer relies on just being big. His hands are fast and violent, and he has a good understanding of when to throw which moves and counters. He is light on his feet for a player pushing 370 pounds. He doesn't have a mean streak in the run game, but in 2023, he was more stout against double teams and got off single blocks more efficiently.
strengths: Sheer size makes him a tough assignment. Pass rush moves and counters were much improved from 2022 to 2023. Really light on his feet for a player pushing 360-plus pounds. Leg drive was powerful in 2023. Held up against double teams in 2023.
weaknesses: Pops up high out of his stance naturally. Conditioning will be naturally tough.
bottom_line: Sweat has the size that you can't teach. At his best, he's an impact, versatile interior defensive player, but weight and conditioning will determine how often that can be in the NFL.

profile: Taylor is built like a super-sized linebacker in the middle, at 6-foot-4 and 305 pounds. His best pass-rush moves come from a good first step and violent hands. However, his strike placement is inconsistent. When he doesn't win by shooting a gap or with a good first step, he can struggle to disengage from blocks. He also has a bad tendency to pop out of his stance and get outleveraged. Taylor is a strong player in run defense, but his lack of consistent leverage allows him to be controlled too easily. Though he is explosive on some reps, he is not necessarily twitched-up when it comes to change of direction, block shedding and pursuit.
strengths: Built like a super-sized linebacker Explosive potential is top tier, though not always consistent Hands can be powerful
weaknesses: Violent and strong, but seems a little out of control when disengaging blocks Hands are powerful, but miss their mark at times While his first step is adequate, he isn't as twitched-up as the best interior defenders Pad level pops up right out of his snap Gets out of his gap too often
bottom_line: When Taylor is on, he possesses the power and explosive athletic ability to be an impact player. We don't see that enough, though. He is a young, hot-and-cold interior defensive lineman — and a talent worth drafting in the top 100 to develop.

profile: The smaller Wingo wins on quickness. His stance is low and loaded, and he can explode off the ball. His hands are well placed, which leads to an effective push-pull, his go-to pass- rush move. But his smaller frame and shorter arms make it tough for him to disengage against better offensive linemen. He has his positive moments in run defense, but his bad plays are too far in the wrong direction. When he has good eye discipline against the run and waits for the back to commit to a lane, he can disengage and make contact at the line of scrimmage. Still, too often he guesses the lane. He also has a bad tendency to get turned around at the line.
strengths: Quick off the snap Violent push-pull move Hand speed and placement are effective. Helps make up for his shorter arms Low and loaded stance before the snap allows him to fire off the ball with power and leverage
weaknesses: Shorter strides make for quick steps but less ground covered Gets moved out of gaps and turned around too easily Stiff to change direction
bottom_line: Wingo's shorter arms and legs limit his efficacy and versatility. He will likely be limited between the 2i and 4i alignments in a 4- 3 scheme. But his quickness and consistent hand placement can lead to some success as a rotational pass rusher in the NFL.

profile: Booker comes from an athletic family, as both his father and mother played sports at the college level. He approaches offensive tackles as if he's a ball handler trying to get to the basket. He has a slender, long frame with above 50th percentile arms, which he uses well to keep tackles at a distance as well as perform push-pull, speed-to-power and long arm moves. His lack of weight is worrisome, though. He does not carry much weight in his lower half, which limits true explosiveness and leg drive. Despite not having much time as a starter, he has a deep pass-rush bag.
strengths: Really slippery for a player with his length — can get across a blocker's face or shoot a gap pretty easily. Pass-rush plan seems to be built around reading what the OT will do before countering. Long limbs and effort make him very annoying to keep blocked (a compliment).
weaknesses: Not much weight in his lower half. Run defense is based around an arm-over to shed the block rather than holding the line of scrimmage. I don't love that he's always waiting for the OT to declare what they're going to do with their hands. Doesn't really have that pop at contact. Need to play with better leverage more consistently.
bottom_line: Booker is an alluring prospect because of his style of pass- rushing, but his lack of weight is a concern. He must play with better pad level to mitigate that at the NFL level.

profile: Braswell is an impressive athlete on the edge. His first-step explosiveness, pursuit speed and natural strength are all starting caliber for the NFL. His speed-to-power bull rush moves even the biggest offensive tackle back at least two or three steps. It has taken him some time to hone his fundamentals to get on the field as a starting outside linebacker — and it didn't help he had Will Anderson Jr. in front of him. He still has some inconsistencies with his hand placement and pass-rush timing, and he needs more counters and better hand usage to get off blocks. Even so, this kind of athlete wins at the professional level.
strengths: A very explosive athlete. Natural strength level is imposing. Has the athleticism to turn and run with tight ends and running backs in coverage when playing an outside linebacker role. Fast hands.
weaknesses: A bit stiff when it comes to turning the corner. Hand usage and precision are inconsistent. Has a false step that could be cleaned up, and he can get happy feet before the snap. Still learning the timing of when to throw certain pass-rush moves.
bottom_line: Even if he doesn't become a pass-rush technician, his power, speed and length present a rotational role as a floor and an impact starter ceiling.

profile: Byrd has taken a long journey from a two-star recruit to an NFL draft prospect in 2024. Byrd's upper body strength is the biggest selling point of his game right now. His push-pull move (while not as twitchy) can ragdoll tight ends and even some offensive linemen. It also helps him hold the line of scrimmage for run defense. However, his technique needs more consistency. He plays a bit too recklessly right now and looks off-balance too often. He also has a repeatable pass- rush path. Sometimes, he's slow off the line and other times, he's trying to go too wide around the arc. His effort and strength are there, but they need to be more repeatable.
strengths: High-effort player who doesn't stop until the whistle is blown. Impactful push-pull move (though it is slower). Really strong upper body.
weaknesses: Effort is there but feels out of control too often. Balance is a bit of an issue, as he needs to keep his feet grounded and underneath him. Take too long to get into his pass rush too often.
bottom_line: Byrd shows promise with good upper body strength as a 3-4 outside linebacker, but his fundamentals must become more consistent to be a reliable depth piece.

profile: Ceasar is a fundamentally sound outside linebacker who brings plenty of experience. Most of his work has come along the defensive line, but he also played some off-ball linebacker and has played both sides on punt and kick teams. He bases his pass-rush profile on a long-arm technique that is moderately effective due to his use of leverage. He has adequate quickness for club and rip moves. However, his length likely won't be something he can consistently win with in the NFL. His strength profile could also be an issue. He can generate push from bull rushes and when defending the run, but that is more due to correct leverage than natural strength.
strengths: No false steps out of his stance. Decent burst to get off the line of scrimmage and upfield. Maintains leverage well enough to be a better run-stopper than expected for a player at his weight. Good ankle flexibility to corner at above-average angles.
weaknesses: Likes to use the long-arm technique but doesn't have the length to win there at the NFL level. Does not have the length to get off blocks consistently. Below-average strength and length for counter moves. Speed-to-power does not generate enough force to be effective. Club moves don't really move the offensive tackle's arms/hands away.
bottom_line: Ceasar projects as a versatile outside linebacker type of edge player who can be productive in a rotational role in late-down situations.

profile: Cole's length is a huge plus in the trenches (99th percentile). His measurables make him a potential 3-4 EDGE, but his explosiveness, lateral quickness and fast hands make him a potential 4-3 DE who can give OTs fits due to his arm length. Despite being 6-foot-6, he is flexible enough to play from a two-point stance. Cole still lacks refinement as a pass-rusher. His win percentage is low because he doesn't have many moves outside of a push-pull, long arm or an attempt at speed-to-power, and he does not get to counters quickly. As a run defender, he needs more lower-body strength to not be moved off the ball as easily.
strengths: Extremely long arms allow him to get into offensive tackles with leverage and control. Powerful push-pull to shed blocks. Long arm is very effective when he gets the hand placement right. Explosive pass-rusher who can get off the line with speed and effort. Active, long arms to get up and bat passes in his rush.
weaknesses: Has a false step, at times, that needs to be cleaned up. Needs counter moves — hands can stop working once he gets engaged with an offensive tackle Struggled in run defense against Texas (lack of anchor).
bottom_line: It's often futile to say a six-year player with low production still has potential, but Cole breaks the mold. His length and athleticism give him front versatility, and if he can gain some extra power and hone in on pass-rush moves in the NFL, he can be a contributing player in some way.

profile: Dorlus is a versatile defensive lineman whom all 32 teams could find a spot for. He played his first two seasons as an interior defender at around 285-290 pounds but has played more as an edge rusher/defensive end at around 280 over the last two years. He is a bit of a tweener but can be a mismatch. He's quick enough to beat interior guards and powerful enough to knock back tackles. He bases his pass- rush plan around a strong punch at contact, whether that be a long arm or a club move. As a run defender, he has the size and strength to set the edge but needs more consistent discipline when doing so.
strengths: OTs are not used to his strength on the edge. Really good punch at contact. Quick enough to win inside and powerful enough to win on the edge. Devastating club move (best paired with the arm-over). Powerful long arm.
weaknesses: High pad level when asked to rush from a two-point stance (shouldn't be doing that much in the league). A bit sloppy with his discipline for run defense. At times, he loses ground he shouldn't.
bottom_line: Though a bit of a tweener, Dorlus has 3-4 and 4-3 versatility with a strong power profile to be a rotational player and potential spot starter.

profile: Khalid Duke's calling card is his effort and his fearlessness. Despite smaller measurables, he never backs down from a challenge. Unfortunately, that lack of size could be a dealbreaker at the NFL level. He is too easily walled off by single blocks and cannot stand against doubles. His lack of arm length prohibits him from keeping his distance and getting locked up by offensive tackles. His hands are fast, but they will have to be even faster to remain successful in the NFL.
strengths: Doesn't back down from any assignment, especially the ones against big OL he knows he will likely lose. Quick push-pull to disengage.
weaknesses: Size is definitely an issue. Single blocks can control him, and he can't hold against doubles. Is thrown on the ground too easily. Doesn't have the strength or length for most pass rush moves in the NFL.
bottom_line: Duke is a high-energy and fearless edge rusher who could be used in pass-rush-specific situations, but his lack of size will limit his rosterability.

profile: Eboigbe is a powerful, versatile player who can line up anywhere from a zero-shade nose tackle to a five-technique defensive end. His size and length are big pluses, especially since he has good hip flexibility to get low in his stance. His pass-rush profile isn't diverse, but his natural strength helps his long-arm and bull-rush moves. He is a great anchor against the run and can be a short-yardage package player. His first step is powerful, but his top gear is average. He doesn't boast much agility or flexibility when changing direction. His hand usage could be more consistent, but when he does hit a swipe, club or rip, it can be effective.
strengths: Ideal size and length for a 3-4 defensive end. Strong anchor at point of attack versus the run. For a player with his height and length, he maintains good pad level for explosive power out of his stance. Strong bull rush. Can eat up double teams without getting blown off the ball. Impactful goal-line/short-yardage player. Hand usage is generally pretty straightforward, but when he goes for swipes, his hands are powerful.
weaknesses: Limited change of direction ability. Not flexible enough to bend around the edge. First step is powerful but has just an average weight-adjusted top gear. Pass rush profile is very strength-dimensional. Hand usage could be better (more swipes, clubs, rips).
bottom_line: Eboigbe brings valuable size and length to the defensive line, and though he likely won't be a consistent pass-rush presence, his strength and size in the run game make for a high-floor player who can be scheme versatile and a valuable mid-round asset.

profile: Elliss comes from an NFL family, and it shows. He's smart and disciplined with his fundamentals, which helps him overcome some strength and length deficiencies. His hands are fast and consistently in the right place inside and at the chest of offensive tackles, which allows him to dictate contact and remain in control, even against stronger players. He has a variety of pass-rush moves, and in 2023, he expanded his repertoire even more with a variety of different swipes and rip combinations. He has an adequate first step for the NFL and can corner better than most in this class.
strengths: Smart hand usage. Hands got even faster in 2023. Improved at mitigating his lack of length in 2023. Pairs fast hands with effective pass-rush moves Flexibility/bend is good for the NFL level. Shifty player, as he always shakes his shoulders to get around blockers.
weaknesses: Lack of length will be an issue as a full-time edge player. Worried about overall strength.
bottom_line: In order for him to remain a difference maker like he was in 2023, he will have to get stronger. If he can add weight but remain as quick and flexible, he can be an impactful pass- rusher.

profile: Green led the country in both sacks and tackles for loss before suffering a season-ending knee injury in 2023. He is just 6-foot-1 and 245 pounds. That means he'll lose the arm- length battle in the NFL, and his shorter strides limit how much ground he can cover. However, he uses his small size to his advantage. He deploys a subtle shoulder dip to get under taller offensive tackles, and he has good change of direction for stunts. His hands are powerful and violent. He has a knack for consistently getting off blocks, but he could stand to develop better hand swipes to not allow offensive tackles to land as many strikes on his chest.
strengths: Low, loaded three-point stance. Smaller height gives way to good leverage when bull rushing. Smaller, feisty, compact frame could actually lead to holding penalties as offensive tackles try to get a hand on him. Fast, violent hands. Nice subtle shoulder dip to get under taller offensive tackles. Effective stunt/game player due to change of direction from his compact build.
weaknesses: Will be one of the smaller defensive ends in the NFL once drafted. Will lose the length battle against NFL offensive tackles. Short strides limit how much ground he can cover (even though those legs are churning). Change of direction is adequate, but his hips and ankles are stiff, and his flexibility is likely below average.
bottom_line: Green comes in a compact build that limits where you can play him as an edge rusher, but he's a feisty player who consistently plays with good natural leverage. You don't want to make a living betting on size outliers, but (pending recovery from knee surgery) he can be a good depth player.

profile: Harrell comes from NFL bloodlines, as his father played for nine years as an NFL linebacker. Harrell followed in his father's footsteps as a linebacker in high school but has played on the edge for Michigan. Harrell wins with natural athleticism that allows him to showcase good body control, lateral quickness and short-area burst. His hands are fast and well-timed to stay off blocks and slip off OTs' shoulders. He also has a nice inside spin move. His lack of length for an edge rusher does show up when offensive tackles can get their hands on him. His power also fades quickly after he makes contact. This also shows up in run defense.
strengths: Well-built athlete with good body control and core strength. Above average stop-and-start ability for change of direction. Can rush from both the left and right side. Fast hands, especially for a two-hand swipe after contact.
weaknesses: Power fades fast versus better offensive tackles. Exclusively a 3-4 OLB. Stiff up the arc; they put him in a wide nine to mitigate that.
bottom_line: Harrell's smaller size and lack of power limit his ceiling as a pass-rusher, but he does have the speed game to be an OLB rush specialist for a 3-4 defense. He may enter the NFL as an edge rusher, but he might end up finding a better role as an off- ball linebacker.

profile: Though a bit undersized (though arm length and wingspan are great for edge) Hunt packs a punch. He is strong at contact and can push back OL or even completely erase TEs. He is very explosive out of his stance to go with decent bend. He lacks a well-rounded pass-rush profile (likely because he didn't really need one to dominate his competition level).
strengths: Good T/E stunt player due to his explosiveness. Quick to get across the face both inside and out. Uniquely long arms for his height (lack thereof). Dense player who can really pack a punch at contact. Impressive pursuit speed. Explosive first step demands OTs make the right first move out of their stance.
weaknesses: Wins primarily due to being a better athlete than his competition. Lacks natural leverage as primarily a stand-up rusher.
bottom_line: Hunt lacks nuance for the position, whether that is in natural leverage, stance or block shedding, but that can all be improved. What he has that you can't teach (explosiveness, length and power) is worth drafting in the mid-rounds to develop as a 3-4 OLB.

profile: Isaac is a very solid edge prospect. First and foremost, he is a stout run defender, even at a low weight. His hand placement and leverage are consistent and effective when holding the line of scrimmage, which allows him to rip off blocks to make tackles after setting the edge. His hands are also active when rushing the passer. He loves the club-rip move, and he uses it consistently to turn the corner and get around blockers quickly. My biggest issue with him stems from concerns about his strength due to his lower weight. His burst and pursuit speed aren't elite, but they are good enough for the next level.
strengths: Fast and violent hands for swipes when rushing the passer. Consistent hand placement to win inside and gain leverage when bull rushing and defending the run. Hands are constantly moving to get off blocks — swipes, rips, clubs. Strong when taking on split-zone blockers coming across the line.
weaknesses: Lower weight percentile shows up when trying to hold his ground in run defense, even against single blocks. Has the weight and measurables of an outside linebacker, but his game is more suited for a defensive end.
bottom_line: If he can pack some extra pounds for added strength and anchor ability while remaining adequately explosive, he has the handwork and pass-rush profile to be an NFL starter.

profile: Now a three-year starter weighing 265 pounds, Jackson has an NFL body type for 4-3 defensive end work. He plays with his hair on fire, as his competitive toughness was a consistent plus in his tape. Though not twitchy, he is explosive with good build-up speed for speed-to-power bull rushes. He also did a good job staying low to maximize explosiveness and leverage for power moves. His hand usage is good for power moves, but he must continue to develop more pass-rush moves. He has the strength to be reliable in run defense, though he does take chances as a gap shoot a bit too much. Shorter arms do hinder his ability to tackle.
strengths: Not the twitchiest player out of his stance, but he has a powerful burst that leads to nice speed-to-power rushes. Low and explosive burst out of his stance leads to good leg drive. Consistent and effective hand placement, especially when bull rushing. Has the strength to totally handle tight ends inline.
weaknesses: Speed/explosiveness is more build-up than sudden. Change of direction flexibility is adequate, but it takes him a few steps to get going. Shorter arms hinder wrapping up tackles. Tries to shoot gaps in the run games rather than hold his run fit a little too often.
bottom_line: Jackson has the power profile and effort of an early rotational 4-3 defensive end with the potential to be a starter at the next level.

profile: Jean-Baptiste's preferred alignment is as a 3-4 outside linebacker, especially given his weight. He brings ideal height to the edge position at just under 6-5, but his arm length doesn't quite match. His first step explosiveness, lateral explosiveness and pursuit speed are all impressive for his size. When he runs and chases, he stands out. However, as a whole, his power profile is lacking. When he gets his hands and leverage right, he can mitigate strength concerns, but he needs to add weight and density to not get pushed around so much in the NFL.
strengths: Good athlete for an edge player. His first step is explosive, and his top speed in pursuit is impressive. Has good pop at contact despite his lower weight. Strong run defender, especially for his size — has the ability to stack and shed pretty quickly. High-effort player.
weaknesses: Lighter weight allows him to be pushed around. Bull rush dies and OTs eventually anchor, but he does get some good push. Height is well above average, but length is just average for the league.
bottom_line: There are flashes of impactful speed rush elements of Jean- Baptiste's game that pave the way for a pass-rush specialist role in the NFL as a 3-4 OLB. He must get stronger if he wants to become more than that.

profile: Johnson is a well-built edge defender who projects as a heavy-handed 4-3 defensive end in an even front or a 3-4 defensive end in an odd front. He isn't the most twitched-up player, but he does have a powerful lower body that creates good build-up speed. He mostly wins with power, either from a long arm, bull rush or a combination of the two. Even so, the rest of his pass-rush profile — both initial moves and counters — is lacking enough depth to be successful in the NFL. There are times when he gains the outside edge against his blocker, but he just doesn't have the refined rip or arm- over move to truly break free and get to the quarterback.
strengths: Doesn't have twitchy speed, but good lower body power to make for good build-up speed. Powerful first step, especially when pinning his ears back. Better bend than you'd expect for a player who is 6-foot-3 and 265 pounds. Explosiveness shows up the most out of a three-point stance.
weaknesses: Does not have much in terms of pass-rush plans or counters. Hand emphasis is lacking, as his hands don't move fast when using his initial moves or getting off blocks. A bit flat-footed when lined up in a two-point stance, as he is not as loaded for explosiveness as others.
bottom_line: Johnson has the mold of an athlete on the edge teams would want to draft and develop, but he must continue to improve his hand speed and usage when rushing the passer and getting off blocks if he is going to get the playing time needed to showcase that above average weight-adjust athletic ability.

profile: Kamara is an outlier for an edge player in his measurables. At 6-foot-1, he's below the fifth percentile for all NFL edge rushers, which comes with natural pros and cons. The pros are he can really explode out of a low, loaded stance with good pad level to fuel his preferred move: a bull rush. The cons is a lack of length, which t makes it more difficult for him to really press offensive linemen in his bull rush. It also holds him back from being able to get off blocks. He's a strong player, though, and has a motor that is always running hot.
strengths: Wins with power. Lower height makes for a natural leverage advantage, which maximizes his power output on bull rushes. Compact, loaded stance allows him to accelerate off his front foot with good pad level.
weaknesses: At 6-foot-1, his length will be an issue. Even with hand moves, it's tough for him to get off blocks due to his lack of length.
bottom_line: Kamara's measurables limit his finesse pass-rush potential and ceiling. However, he can be a stout depth defensive lineman due to how much he enjoys the physical aspect of the position.

profile: Kneeland's film looks like a car crash from an action movie — in a good way. He puts his big body on the line every snap, and he doesn't want to run around his blockers; he wants to run through them. His pass-rush profile is built around an all- out bull rush. He also likes to combine his gap-shooting ability with a good first step and a violent rip move to get free. He has been an impactful run defender, making frequent tackles for loss. He's a bit stiff when it comes to changing direction and doesn't have the deepest bag of pass-rush moves, as he prefers to win with strength more than finesse.
strengths: Impressive burst for a player at his weight. Unique build that comes with ideal arm length. Pass rush profile is based on imposing strength and converting speed-to-power. Doesn't just want to run around blockers; he wants to run through them. Relentless motor.
weaknesses: Stiff when changing direction. Lacks flexibility. Frenetic style can be reckless, at times. Not a very deep pass rush arsenal.
bottom_line: Overall, his competition wasn't the best, but he absolutely dominated it, especially in 2023. NFL teams will love his passion for physicality. He has the body, explosiveness and mentality of an NFL contributor.

profile: Latu, who suffered a neck injury in 2021 that almost ended his football career, was the most productive pass rusher in college football over the past two seasons. His hand usage is fantastic — fast, precise and, most importantly, with purpose. He has a wide variety of pass-rush moves and counters that appear second nature to him. He is also a versatile edge defender, playing a near-even split of left- and right-side snaps with a good mix of two- and three-point stances. He is just an adequate athlete with sub-50th-percentile arm length. He could also stand to add some density and strength to improve anchor ability and tackling.
strengths: Hands are precise, fast and, most importantly, planned Quickness and agility are a nightmare for interior offensive linemen Vast repertoire of pass-rush moves Eyes are always in the backfield for the ball Above-average bend/corner ability
weaknesses: Length is adequate but not an advantage First step is adequate, but he won't be blowing by NFL tackles His higher PFF run-blocking grade is due to shooting gaps more than truly holding the line of scrimmage
bottom_line: Overall, though somewhat limited athletically, his home is in the offensive backfield due to his hand usage and pass rush moves that will continue to win at the NFL level.

profile: Linton has a slender build, which gives him both pros and cons as an outside linebacker-type edge rusher. He has long arms and legs to cover ground up the arc when speed rushing on the outside, and he combines that with an effective long-arm pass-rush plan. However, his lower weight profile shows up in troublesome ways. He just does not have the density to hold up as an early down defender at the NFL level — his run defense effectiveness stems from shooting gaps. There are also some durability concerns due to him playing in the trenches below 240 pounds.
strengths: Fast player with a slender build. Good arm length despite his height being a bit fabricated on the team's website. Good flexibility and change-of-direction ability at his lower weight.
weaknesses: Slender size is an issue in terms of strength and durability. Gap shooting run defender more than a hold-the-line kind of player.
bottom_line: Linton is a finesse pass-rusher with good agility and flexibility to pair with adequate length for the position, but his lack of size and strength likely limit him strictly to a pass-rush specialist role.

profile: McGregor is tall, but his arm length does not match his height. He likes to use length moves right now (long arm, stab, speed-to-power bull rush) but will struggle to win like that against NFL OTs. He has a good first step and decent bend to get around the arc on third downs. His hand placement is generally quick and precise, and his two-hand swipe is effective. He is a fundamentally sound run defender but lacks the true size/strength to set the edge. He is a smart player who understands the little things about the game.
strengths: Very quick two-hand swipe. Conscious hand placement and leverage to get blockers on their heels (on skates against tight ends). Versatile rusher who can play on the left and right side of the line. Good (not elite) first step to get up the arc. Smart player — eyes are always looking for the ball, hands get up to bat passes, and he generally knows when to disengage.
weaknesses: Tall but does not have the arm length to match. Speed-to-power stalls quickly due to lower weight. Likes to win with length moves, but it will be tough to do so against NFL OTs.
bottom_line: McGregor has the mindset of a future NFL player to stick around in the league in a 3-4 scheme but may lack the length and strength needed to ever be a consistent starter.

profile: Gabriel Murphy projects as a specialized outside linebacker type of edge pass rusher at the next level. He is undersized for the position and will have trouble overcoming length deficiencies in the NFL. However, he has lightning-quick hands with a technician's mindset. He has a good understanding of how and why to attack the half-man — reducing his strength and size limitations. He also shows a plethora of pass-rush plans (using speed and quickness as his foundation to win) with a good amount of counters, which he executes quickly (almost second nature).
strengths: Technical, controlled player. Has a good pass-rush plan and is quick to counter. Really fast with his counters, especially in 2023. Hands are fast and well placed inside for initial contact when bull rushing. Great understanding of how to always attack the half-man.
weaknesses: Not an imposing athlete — strength, density and explosiveness are just adequate or below average by NFL standards. Will not win with length at the NFL level. Can get pushed around versus guards when lined up inside. Has a good punch at contact but doesn't have strong leg drive to continue to beat an offensive tackle's anchor.
bottom_line: Murphy is lacking in physical gifts, but he mitigates that with fantastic hand usage and a wisdom of what works as a pass- rusher to find a rotational contributing role as an on-ball outside linebacker in the NFL.

profile: Grayson Murphy, as you may expect, has a very similar build and skill set to his twin brother, Gabriel. Both win with good hand usage and a variety of pass-rush moves. Grayson, like his brother, has limited arm length and overall athleticism (explosiveness, strength, and lack of top-tier flexibility). Grayson appears to win more with strength whereas his brother wins more with quickness. Grayson likes to use the bull rush as the foundation of his pass rush play and evolves from there as the game goes on.
strengths: Like to use the bull rush with good leverage to push the pocket. Decent anchor ability for a player who weighs less than 260 lbs. A little stronger than his brother, Gabriel.
weaknesses: Not an imposing athlete — strength, density, explosiveness all just adequate or below average. Length adequate at best for the NFL level. Decent first step to threaten the outside shoulder but doesn’t have the bend to corner. Bull rush is strong in its first two steps, but lack of length makes it easier for OTs to anchor and stop him
bottom_line: Overall, Grayson Murphy is not imposing with his speed or strength, but he is a more advanced pass-rusher with good initial pass-rush moves (based on strength) and fundamentals as a run defender to make for a good depth edge player.

profile: Eyabi Okie-Anoma has good natural athletic ability, specifically in his speed-to-power pass-rush profile. However, he lacks the counter moves when the initial move stalls. His motor also seems to run hot and cold — when it's hot, he's a handful. His footwork can sometimes be all over the place, which messes up his ability to consistently get upfield as fast as he can.
strengths: Good acceleration when he pins his ears back to rush. Nice speed-to-power move.
weaknesses: First step is average at best. At times he can false step out of his stance. When he goes all out, he's tough to handle, but he needs to play that way more often. Played at five schools in six years. Doesn't have the counters to continue to work once his initial move stalls.
bottom_line: Eyabi Okie-Anoma is a talented player with a complicated college football past. He remains a developmental edge rusher with good speed-to-power potential, but his game still needs a lot of refinement.

profile: Robinson is an alien-like athlete. He has some jaw-dropping plays where he can fire off the line and get into the backfield with ease. However, outside of his first step and fast hands, he is an incomplete pass rusher. Most of his backfield production comes from him feasting off an inferior tackle, if he's facing one that week. He could also struggle with length against NFL-caliber tackles. His pass-rush profile needs to expand, as he does not have a regular rotation of pass-rush moves or counters when he doesn't win with athleticism off the jump. He is a strong run defender but has some reps where he gets out of his gap to try to make a play.
strengths: Naturally low and loaded stance. Explodes off the front foot with consistency. Elite first-step explosiveness and acceleration up the arc.
weaknesses: Lack of length will likely be a consistent issue for him. Does not have an adequate amount of counters to get off blocks. Shorter strides make for good explosiveness and early acceleration, but he doesn't cover a ton of ground when getting up the arc. Gets locked up when defending the run against Tes too often. Hand usage/placement needs consistency.
bottom_line: Regardless of his lack of polish, Robinson is a gifted player athletically — likely on a level that is top of the class. A lot of what leaves you wanting more from Robinson is coachable. Unlocking that is the key for him to go from a boom-or-bust athlete to a dominant edge defender.

profile: Robinson has the build of an NFL-type defensive lineman. He spent most of his early years at Missouri as a defensive tackle. He didn't have the typical build of an interior defensive lineman with long arms and a weight profile just above 300 pounds, but his strength allowed him to survive there. In 2023, he moved to edge out of necessity and had his most productive season. His strength on the edge was dominant, as he demolished tight ends and was even able to ragdoll offensive tackle with a violent push-pull move. He has below- average speed, agility and flexibility, but his weight-adjusted explosiveness could still be a strong score.
strengths: Length is a big plus. Bull rush is imposing, even against inferior offensive linemen. You can't single-block this guy with a tight end. When he uses a push-pull technique, he can actually corner well.
weaknesses: First-step explosiveness is below average for NFL edge defenders. Will not threaten the outside shoulder with speed or bend. Below average change of direction acceleration.
bottom_line: Robinson is a powerful lineman who can line up anywhere from zero- to a seven-technique. He won't win with speed much at the next level, but he certainly can with power. His strength profile projects to a rotational role as a floor with starting potential if he can continue to hone in on his pass-rush plans.

profile: Solomon may not pass the "off the bus" eye test for an NFL edge defender, but he fits the bill as an athlete. He has gained more than 30 pounds since his high school recruiting days and moved from outside linebacker to defensive end throughout his college career. He has a good first step to get off the ball, but his flexibility and change-of-direction ability to give bigger offensive tackles fits are even more impressive.
