weaknesses: Man coverage ability is there in flashes but is inconsistent Straight-line speed is good, not great Can be a bit overaggressive in pursuit angles
bottom_line: Hicks is a well-built strong safety who can play at all three levels of the field. He is a tone-setting tackler and has starting potential in two-safety systems, especially as a strong safety/robber over the middle.

profile: As a true freshman, Kinchens played in all 12 games, starting the final five. He then became a full-time starter in 2022 and 2023. Kinchens is a good all-around athlete who has made plays in both the run and pass games. Most of his experience and production is from a free safety spot, including 12 interceptions. His range from a single-high role is good, but a big boon to that is his anticipation rather than rare athletic ability. In the run game, he is willing and in control, but his lower weight shows up in the form of missed tackles. He just doesn't pack a big punch at contact.
strengths: Adequate overall athlete Good eyes in zone when watching the quarterback Impressive ball skills at the catch point
weaknesses: Lighter weight/frame shows up when tackling downhill A little reserved when coming downhill to tackle Has lapses in judgment when in zone Explosion and change of direction are decent but not great Taller posture in his backpedal. Doesn't seem to affect his change-of-direction ability much
bottom_line: Kinchens is a solid all-around athlete with a good eye for where quarterbacks are going with the ball. He possesses great ball skills to come down with interceptions when he anticipates throws. A little lighter in size, he is projected as a potential starter at free safety.

profile: Mustapha is a throwback tone-setter over the middle of the field. His measurables and mentality are reminiscent of Bob Sanders. Unfortunately, he doesn't have the plus athletic ability — specifically, fluidity and top speed — of Sanders. He does his best work coming from a two-deep safety shell where he can keep the play in front of him and fire downhill when needed. He is an all-out blitzer, even from a deep safety spot. His shorter arms can cause problems when wrapping up tackles, but when he hits players, they feel it.
strengths: Will hit with everything he's got Mentality for physical play stands out in run defense, blitzing and coverage Can play fast yet decently in control when coming downhill from depth
weaknesses: Desire for hit power leads to missed tackles, at times Shorter arms affect tackling ability, especially when flying in at high speeds Side shuffles to retreat deep, likely to avoid backpedal and turning his hips
bottom_line: Mustapha has the skill set and mentality of a throwback strong safety. He does not have the fluidity or long speed to be relied upon in single-high roles, but his toughness, power and motor make him an ideal depth safety to draft and develop, likely starting with a special teams role.

profile: After committing to Minnesota, Nubin waited his turn behind Antoine Winfield Jr. before becoming a full-time starter in 2021. Since then, he's become Minnesota's all-time leader in interceptions (13). His athleticism — an explosive first step, controlled and quick footwork and fluid hips — provides him with good range in coverage from a free safety role. He pairs that with good eyes and anticipation for where passes and ball carriers are going. In run defense, he is consistently willing to be physical but tends to lead with the crown of his helmet. He also can be a bit overaggressive in pursuit angles.
strengths: Quick, controlled backpedal Good first-step explosiveness Desire to make impactful hits on ball carriers/pass catchers Impressive ability to flip his hips to run Effective blitzer, even from deep alignments Top-tier ball skills for a safety Excellent eyes/anticipation for where the ball is going
weaknesses: Leads with the crown of his helmet too much Lighter run defender Can be overaggressive in pursuit angles
bottom_line: Nubin possesses the athleticism, football IQ and run-defense potential to be a versatile and impactful safety in any scheme, though he would likely make the most plays in a system that consistently uses two-deep coverages, allowing him to play free, robber and box safety roles.

profile: Oladapo is a team captain and multi-year starter. His size is a big plus, and he has more fluidity in his change of direction than most safeties who try to play at that size. He's a strong tackler but does fail to wrap up at times. His ball skills are lacking, but he can still play close coverage and be physical in man enough to warrant incompletions and drops. He doesn't have a ton of ball production, but he'll be more of a box defender anyway. He is also a good nickel option against tight ends in the slot.
strengths: Is a more fluid mover than safeties who try to play the position around his size. Good athleticism to match up against tight ends in man coverage. Good pre-snap communicator. Has the size and speed to play around the edge as a blitzer and on the goal line.
weaknesses: Has decently long arms but still fails to wrap up sometimes. Bigger frame comes with a natural weakness against quicker route runners. Top gear is lacking and will limit him in range on the back end.
bottom_line: Oladapo brings unique agility and fluidity to the position at his size. He has the body to play in the box as well as split safety duties on the back end, but his long speed limits his range to a two-safety system.

profile: Owens is an incredibly gifted athlete. His size/speed combination is rare. His power at contact (due to his explosive movements) is imposing for ball carriers. He can also recover when beat in coverage better than most. His combination of measurables and athleticism make him an ideal match for tight ends in man coverage. He has only started one year of college ball, likely due to his lack of anticipation. Whether it's in run defense or coverage, he is often slow to recognize where the play is going and relies too heavily on his athleticism to make up for it. His pursuit angles could also stand to be more direct.
strengths: Has the size and athleticism to cover tight ends in man coverage. His contact when the ball arrives is imposing. Movement skills and explosiveness are hard to believe at his size. Plays at the linebacker level quite a bit, which could be his calling in the league. Speed-to-power hits are imposing and can dislodge the ball.
weaknesses: Anticipation in coverage could be better (though his athleticism makes up for it). Needs better flow recognition for where the ball carrier is going when defending the run. Pursuit angles could be more direct. Larger body makes it tougher to flip the hips in deep free safety coverage.
bottom_line: Owens is light on experience and polish, but his physical gifts are truly rare. He might be more of a linebacker at the next level, but this is the kind of player you take early on Day 3 just because his potential doesn't come around often.

profile: Proctor is not afraid to come up and tackle. Whether he's at the second level, creeping down as a strong safety or even playing from depth as a free safety, if it's a run play, he's rallying to it with pace. Sometimes he does come in too hot, which affects tackling efficiency. He has the length and the physical style to be a good man coverage defender against running backs and tight ends. As for ball skills, it's a total toss-up whether or not he'll come down with a pick, as he had more dropped interceptions in his career than interceptions.
strengths: Will come from depth to make tackles at the line of scrimmage or in the backfield. Played Malachi Corley pretty well in man coverage. He wants to make the play — whether that's combined tackles, solo tackles or PBUs. Good short-area control to not miss a tackle or be fooled on options.
weaknesses: Anticipation makes it look like he's faster than he is. Love his eagerness to make tackles, but he can come in too reckless and miss wrapping up. Has more dropped interceptions in his career than interceptions.
bottom_line: Proctor is a versatile safety who has a physical mentality that every team would like to draft on Day 3 as a depth and special teams player.

profile: When Simpson arrived at Auburn, he weighed just 160 lbs. He played cornerback for four seasons before moving to more of a safety role in 2023. Simpson was a below-average athlete for a wide CB, specifically in his run-and-change speed. But that isn't the case at safety. He shows decent long speed for range and plus fluidity for change of direction. This translates well to slot coverage assignments from his safety spot. He is still learning spacing, both in coverage and run fits. His biggest issues stem from his weight when he is asked to be physical, in both man coverage and tackling. NFL tight end assignments will be tougher for him.
strengths: CB movement skills come in handy when changing direction and covering ground Footwork/corner skills translate to slot coverage Attacks the ball in the air for forced incompletions
weaknesses: Lack of weight shows up when asked to be physical/tackle Still getting the hang of spacing from the backend Plays very upright. High pad level Athleticism is below average for a cornerback, adequate for a safety
bottom_line: Simpson's cornerback background gives him good versatility as a free safety/slot defender in two-deep safety systems. His overall size would make him an outlier as a contributor, but his movement skills give him a shot to be that as a Day 3 developmental player.

profile: Taylor, who is the cousin of Hall of Fame safety Ed Reed, won the Jim Thorpe Award as the best defensive back in college football in 2023. He is a versatile safety who can interchange between free and strong safety roles. He has a good feel for where the ball is going and is a well-timed blitzer as well. As an athlete, he is balanced and in control of his movement. His issues stem from his long speed. If he is ever in trail, likely from the slot, it is tough for him to catch up. He really needs to keep things in front of him to make a play.
strengths: Looks comfortable in both free and strong safety alignments. Will do the dirty work to take on lead blockers to fit the run. Makes well-timed blitzes. Has good all-around athleticism to seem in control at all times — no recklessness to his game.
weaknesses: Doesn't have great recovery/long speed. Has to keep everything in front of him to make a play.
bottom_line: Taylor has decent all-around size, body control and football intelligence to put himself in the right positions consistently. His lack of a top gear limits how much he can be relied upon as a backend defender, but he can be a solid depth and special teams defensive back.

profile: Taylor-Demerson is a high-football-IQ type of free safety who calculates space and timing well on the back end. He can bait quarterbacks into throws and cut off vertical routes with good anticipation. He has adequate speed for pursuit angles, but his good long speed is more build-up speed. There is a lack of suddenness with changing direction, which is a concern. He plays with a lot of control, but that sometimes comes off as playing slower than what will be required in the pros. He can be a reliable tackle but slows down for tackles, opting not to take chances to miss, which sometimes leads to a lack of physicality.
strengths: Constant pre-snap communicator Adequate long speed in pursuit Has some really impressive plays where he anticipates to make plays on the ball Inate feel for spacing and timing on the backend
weaknesses: Feet are heavy and late when aligned in the slot Doesn't always play at a high speed Lacks true single-high athleticism Pursuit angles can be too rounded. He is not a super sudden player Slows down to tackle and dips his head too often
bottom_line: Taylor-Demerson sees the back end of coverage with excellent vision and anticipation. However, his overall play speed must improve to make plays at the NFL level.

profile: Vaki is one of the most unique prospects in the 2024 class. He played both sides of the ball (running back, slot receiver and safety) in high school. He was recruited in the 2019 class, so he is an older prospect, but he has only two years of college football experience due to going on a two-year church mission before playing football for Utah. His straight- line explosiveness is impressive. He has some of the best click-and-close pursuit speed of any safety in the class. He also hits like a truck. He brings versatility, with experience in the slot, in the box and at free safety.
strengths: Impressive top-speed and straight-line acceleration Click-and-close ability stands out when triggering downhill Likes to be physical from the slot When he hits players, they move back Reps at running back are very impressive
weaknesses: Hips are a bit stiff Shorter strides Straight-line athleticism doesn't translate to confidence from a free safety role
bottom_line: While Vaki is very athletic in linear areas, his hips are a bit stiff, so the NFL team that drafts him should limit putting him in situations where he has to change direction and track deep as a free safety. As a primary slot/box safety in zone roles, however, he can be an impact player.

profile: Williams' scouting report starts with his rare size. At just over 6-foot-4 and 230 pounds, he is 99th percentile in both height and weight for the safety position. His size means he is suitable for playing at the second level and blitzing off the edge. It also means he has the potential to hang with tight ends in man coverage. Where he is athletic, he does not consistently show it. He shows a quickness to break on ball carrier in pursuit, but his timing and speed to break on a receiver's route with them lagging. He can also get heavy and slow feet when lining defenders up in space.
strengths: Certainly big enough to play in the box at the second level Ideal measurables to cover tight ends as a nickel defender Really impressive size-speed combination
weaknesses: Not very comfortable when asked to play in single-high or two- high situations. He wants to keep his eyes in front of him Not a great feel for zone responsibilities Fast to break on a running back in pursuit but slow to break on a receiver's route in coverage Feet can get in quicksand when he is lining up a ball carrier in space
bottom_line: Williams brings a rare build to the safety position, but his reaction timing and feel for zone coverage need improving. However, he can be drafted right away as a potential chess piece to try to match against receiving tight ends in man coverage.
